R/main.R sources the scripts in this order: setup.R (which sources code_lists.R), functions.R, create_cohort.R, create_covariates.R, create_outcomes.R, fit_models.R, plot_style.R, tables.R, figures.R. USRDS files are reached only through usRds, located by usRds::set_USRDS_wd() on the machine that holds them. Until usRds#22 is fixed, columns are chosen with select() after load_usrds_file() rather than with its col_select.

Design choices in the code

Stays, not records. All hospitalization records of a person with any cryptococcosis record are combined into stays (collapse_stays()) before anything else, so a code on one record of an overlapping stay counts for the whole stay.
Exclusions only in the flowchart. build_cohort_candidates() computes flags but drops no one; every exclusion is an fc_filter() step, so Figure 1 reproduces the cohort exactly. Box labels are built from the constants in setup.R.
One person, one row from the candidates step on. Joins declare their expected relationships, so an unexpected duplicate stops the run.
Release-dependent names in one place. The UNOS key names differ between USRDS releases; the scripts take them from unos_registration_id and unos_followup_id in setup.R.
Missing is not “no”. Combining yes/no values uses any_known(), so a person with only unknown rejection codes is missing rather than “no”, and a registration with no drug records is missing rather than “not on”.
One row per person for survival. All covariates are fixed and death is the only event, so survfit() takes one row per person; the usRds cohort functions, built for time-varying data, are not used.
Logic in tested functions, loading in scripts. The scripts load data through usRds and call functions from functions.R; the functions are tested on synthetic data in tests/test-functions.R.

Tests
tests/test-functions.R tests every helper on synthetic data with known answers, including boundary dates (window edges, a stay admitted on or spanning the transplant date, birthdays). Run with testthat::test_file("tests/test-functions.R") from the project root. The scripts themselves need usRds and the USRDS files and are not run by the unit tests.
tests/run_synthetic.R runs the whole of R/main.R end to end on an invented USRDS folder written by tests/make_synthetic_usrds.R (Parquet files in the layout usRds maps; every value made up, none derived from records). It points usRds at that folder for the session only and sets death_data_end_date for the synthetic run. Its tables and figures land in the gitignored tables/ and figures/ folders like real ones; they contain no restricted data but are not committed either.

Website
One page per script in quarto/, importing labelled sections with knitr::read_chunk(); the site never runs analysis code. Published by .github/workflows/publish.yml to gh-pages.

title: Statistical methods
text: This page explains the statistical methods in plain language, for readers who want to know what the numbers mean before reading how they were computed. The choices themselves are on the Study design and methods page and in the analysis plan.

title: Statistical methods
text:
Comparing survivors and non-survivors
Tables 1 and 2 compare the people who were alive 6 months after admission with those who had died. For a measurement such as age, the table gives the average and the spread (standard deviation), and the P value comes from a t test of whether the averages differ. For a yes-or-no characteristic, it gives the number and percentage, and the P value comes from a chi-squared test, or from Fisher’s exact test when the numbers are small. A P value is a measure of how surprising a difference would be if there were no real difference; it is not the size of the difference, and with dozens of comparisons some small P values are expected by chance.

title: Statistical methods
text:
Odds ratios from logistic regression
Logistic regression estimates how each characteristic is associated with death within 6 months, taking the others into account. Its result for each characteristic is an odds ratio: how many times higher the odds of death are with the characteristic than without it. An odds ratio of 2 doubles the odds; 1 means no difference. When an outcome is common, as here, where about one in five died1, an odds ratio is further from 1 than the corresponding ratio of risks: above 1 it overstates the risk ratio and below 1 it understates it, so an odds ratio of 2 does not mean twice the risk2,3. The study is descriptive: an odds ratio is an association, not evidence that the characteristic causes death.

title: Statistical methods
text:
Choosing the variables: backward elimination
The paper examined each variable on its own first and then entered them into a multivariable model with backward elimination, removing variables until every remaining one had P below 0.051. It does not list the candidates; this project takes every characteristic in Tables 1 and 2 as one, and removes them one at a time, each time the one with the largest P value (analysis plan, §8). Backward elimination is common. It has known weaknesses: which variables survive can change with small changes in the data, the estimates of those that survive tend to be too far from 1, and their P values and confidence intervals look more certain than they are4,5. Screening variables one at a time first can also drop important ones6. This project keeps the method because its aim is to repeat the paper, and it also refits the paper’s own final model so the estimates can be compared directly (Table 4). The plan lists these limits (§11).
Two details follow Stata’s stepwise command7; the paper reports using Stata 16.1 as well as R1. A characteristic with several categories, such as region, is tested as a whole with one joint test rather than category by category. And every step uses the same people: everyone with all the candidate characteristics known.

title: Statistical methods
text:
Checking the model’s fit
The Hosmer–Lemeshow test groups people by their predicted risk of death and compares predicted with observed deaths in each group8. A small P value suggests the model’s predictions do not match what happened; a large one does not prove that they do.

title: Statistical methods
text:
Survival over time
The Kaplan–Meier method estimates the proportion still alive at each time after admission, using everyone for as long as they were followed, including people whose follow-up ended before they died9. Figure 2 follows the KMunicate recommendations: the curve is shown with its 95% confidence band, and a table beneath it gives the numbers at risk, censored and dead at each time shown10.

title: Statistical methods
text:
Small numbers
Under the USRDS data use agreement no count from 1 to 10 may be published, including one that could be worked out from other numbers (see Data sources). The tables hide such counts, and the survival curve stops before fewer than 11 people remain at risk.

title: Statistical methods
text:
Reporting
Reporting follows STROBE, the guideline for observational studies11, and its extension for studies of routinely collected health data such as billing records, RECORD12.

Project documentsAnalysis plan Code

Scope and reporting framework
This document is the authoritative specification of the study’s scientific objectives, population, definitions, estimands and statistical methods. ARCHITECTURE.md documents the implementation, AGENTS.md the working conventions, and GitHub Issues the open decisions and implementation status. Neither file supersedes this plan.
The analysis replicates a published study1 as the paper describes it, using the usRds package wherever it can do a step, to assess the package’s coverage. The paper and its Supplementary Table 1 are the specification. The original analysis was run in Stata, and that code is no longer available; a later R Markdown reconstruction (2025-03-25) is used only as secondary evidence of how a step may have been done. Where the paper is silent, the plan records an open decision rather than adopting the reconstruction’s choice unexamined. The published estimates are a reference point, not a target. How each step maps to usRds is in references/usrds-coverage.md.
Reporting will follow STROBE2 and RECORD3. The reporting map in §12 links each checklist item to a section of this plan.

1. Objective

Primary: estimate all-cause mortality within 6 months of the index cryptococcosis hospitalization among adult kidney transplant recipients hospitalized under Medicare, 2006–2016.
Secondary:

describe time from kidney transplant to the index hospitalization;
estimate the association of clinical, transplant and immunosuppression characteristics with 6-month mortality.

Methodological (this project): assess, step by step, whether usRds does what the paper’s methods require (covered, partial or gap).

All analyses are exploratory, as in the paper. No hypotheses are tested confirmatorily.

2. Design
Retrospective cohort of kidney transplant recipients, entering at their first post-transplant cryptococcosis hospitalization (the index hospitalization). The question is predictive and descriptive (which factors are associated with death), not causal. Target-trial emulation is not used.

3. Data source

Database: United States Renal Data System standard analysis files, with linked Medicare claims and UNOS transplant records. The release is recorded with each result. The paper used a release covering 2006–2016 claims.
Files:

core: patients, tx, payer history;
hospitalization: hosp_to2009, hosp_2010on;
institutional and physician/supplier claims;
UNOS: txunos_trr_ki, txunos_trr_kp, txfuunos_ki, txfuunos_kp, txirunos.

Observation window: index hospitalizations admitted 2006-01-01 to 2016-12-31. Deaths are ascertained through the release’s death-date currency.
Linkage: by USRDS_ID, as provided by USRDS. Transplant status comes from USRDS core and UNOS files, not diagnosis codes.
Secondary-data declaration: the investigators have analysed these data before (the published study). Results from this reconstruction will be compared with the paper only to check package behaviour.

The index hospitalization and its stay-level variables (diagnoses, procedures, ICU and CCU days, discharge status) come from the USRDS hospitalization files, hosp_to2009 and hosp_2010on (decided in #1). These files are a subset of the institutional claims, restricted to inpatient stays without payment variables (Researcher’s Guide 2024, Appendix B), so institutional claims are not used as a second source for the index stay.

4. Study population
Source population: recipients of a kidney or kidney–pancreas transplant in the USRDS tx file. Exclusions are applied in this order, and each becomes one flowchart step (Figure 1):

Hospitalizations with a cryptococcosis diagnosis code (§5) in any diagnosis position, admitted 2006-01-01 to 2016-12-31.
Restrict to people in the transplant file.
Exclude hospitalizations admitted before the patient’s first kidney transplant. A hospitalization admitted before the transplant is a cryptococcosis hospitalization claim preceding it, which the paper excludes; this includes stays that begin before the transplant and end after it (decided under #4; the reconstruction kept such stays with time since transplant set to 0).
Exclude people with any cryptococcosis claim before their first kidney transplant. Hospital records and physician/supplier claims both count, as the paper says (“physician or hospitalization”), and one claim is enough (decided under #4). A single claim is the usual choice for excluding an earlier condition, where missing a true earlier case matters more than excluding a few people over a rule-out code4. A claim dated on the transplant day is not before it. The paper also excludes claims “before the study period”; the data begin on 2006-01-01, so there are none to find.
Keep each person’s first remaining cryptococcosis hospitalization (the index hospitalization).
Restrict to age 18–90 years on the index admission date.

No separate Medicare-primary restriction is applied. The paper describes the cohort as recipients “with Medicare as their primary insurance coverage” but gives no window or method, and the index hospitalization is itself a Medicare-paid record. The plan therefore treats Medicare-primary status as a consequence of the data source rather than an applied exclusion (decided in #3). An explicit restriction is described as a variation in §9.
The paper does not state the order of step 6 relative to the others. The order above puts claim-based exclusions first, so each later step’s denominator is a set of people with an index hospitalization.

6. Comparator or matching
Not applicable. Comparisons are between people who died within 6 months and those who survived.

7. Outcomes

Primary: death from any cause within 180 days of the index admission date (DIED from the patients file), with the admission day as day 0. A death on day 180 counts, and so does a death on the admission day.
Secondary:

time from index admission to death, censored at the release’s death-date currency (death_data_end_date in R/setup.R, set by whoever runs the analysis for the release in use; the paper does not state it). Every covariate is fixed and death is the only event, so the survival data has one row per person;
time from most recent kidney transplant to index admission.

8. Statistical analysis

Descriptive:

Table 1: characteristics by 6-month vital status;
Table 2: immunosuppression by 6-month vital status;
continuous variables as mean (SD), and median (IQR) for time since transplant;
categorical variables as n (%), with small cells suppressed (§10);
missingness reported per variable;
tables and figures in the style shared by Open Forum Infectious Diseases, Clinical Infectious Diseases and the Journal of Infectious Diseases, which follow the AMA Manual of Style, 11th edition (OFID author guidelines): P values without a leading zero, confidence intervals written “a to b”, table footnotes marked with lowercase letters, and abbreviations defined in the footnotes.

Tests: Student t test for continuous variables; χ² test, or Fisher exact test for sparse tables. Two-sided α = 0.05, with no adjustment for multiple comparisons1.
Survival: Kaplan–Meier curve of time to death from the index admission, with a 6-month reference line (Figure 2).
Model: logistic regression for 6-month mortality.

Every characteristic in Tables 1 and 2 is a candidate (model_candidates in R/setup.R), in the form the paper’s model reports: age as 60 or older1, time since transplant as more than 2 years, and tacrolimus as “not on” at transplant and at follow-up.
Each candidate is first tested alone, then all are entered into a multivariable model with backward elimination: the term with the largest P value is removed while P ≥ .05. The paper reports no entry threshold and no forced variables.
P values for elimination are joint Wald tests, one per term, as in Stata’s stepwise (the paper reports using Stata 16.1 and R). The sample is fixed at the complete cases for all candidates, as Stata does.
Fit is assessed by the Hosmer–Lemeshow test, with deciles of predicted risk.
Adjusted odds ratios with 95% CIs are shown as a forest plot (Figure 3).
The paper’s final model is also fitted as published: its eight terms (cirrhosis, ICU admission, dialysis before transplant, not on tacrolimus at follow-up, age 60 or older, acute kidney injury, more than 2 years since transplant, and an earlier hospitalization for a transplant complication; published_model in R/setup.R)1. It uses the same people as the backward elimination, because the paper’s estimates come from the end of that selection. Table 4 sets its odds ratios beside the published ones, with whether the elimination kept each term. This separates differences in the estimates from differences in which variables the selection keeps.
Backward elimination is kept to mirror the paper. Its limitations are noted in §11.

Missing data: complete-case, as in the paper. The number excluded from the model is reported.
Software: R, with usRds (version and commit recorded with each result), survival, and flowchart for Figure 1.

9. Sensitivity analyses
Variation: explicit Medicare-primary restriction. One way the study could have been done differently is to require Medicare as primary payer from the payer history file (for example on the index admission date, for 365 days before it, or from first transplant to admission), with usRds::verify_medicare_primary(). This tests whether recipients with another primary payer, but a Medicare-paid index stay, change the estimates; it adds a flowchart step the paper does not show (#3).
Alternative: acute rejection from claims. Rejection is measured from UNOS records (§5). The paper’s Methods also mention ICD codes for graft rejection; a claims definition (a hospitalization with ICD-10-CM T86.11, kidney transplant rejection) is an alternative, noted but not built. ICD-9-CM has no rejection-specific kidney code (996.81 covers any complication of a transplanted kidney), so it would apply only from October 2015.
No other sensitivity analyses are prespecified. A comparison of the hospitalization files with institutional claims was considered and not adopted, because the former are a subset of the latter (§3, #1).

10. Disclosure control
The USRDS data use agreement governs. No cell, count or percentage that discloses 1–10 people is published, including counts recoverable by subtraction. Figures, tables and the flowchart stay out of the repository until USRDS review before publication clears them.

11. Limitations to address in reporting

Case and CM definitions use diagnosis codes, without microbiological confirmation.
Immunosuppression during the index stay is not captured.
Stepwise selection gives optimistic P values and unstable selection; the results are exploratory.
Restriction to Medicare-paid hospitalizations limits generalisability, and Medicare-primary status is assumed rather than verified (§4).
Earlier cryptococcosis (§4, step 4) can only be seen while a person had Medicare before transplant. Recipients on dialysis usually did; those transplanted before dialysis, or with other insurance, may have no earlier claims to find, so the exclusion catches more people who had been on dialysis.
Differences from the published estimates may come from the data release, the order of exclusions, the open decisions above, or details of the original Stata code that the paper does not report. They are reported as such, not as corrections to the paper.

title: Code lists
text:
PendingProvisional



Text highlighted like this is provisional: it depends on a decision the analysis plan has not yet made.
This script holds every diagnosis, procedure and billing code list the analysis uses. By the maintainer’s decision, the lists come from the 2025-03-25 reconstruction of the original analysis rather than from Supplementary Table 1 of the paper1. The two are identical except for diabetes and the HCPCS drug codes (below). After every code was checked against the official code sets, a few corrections were made, also below.

title: Code lists
text:
One table of codes
All lists are in one table, code_lists, with one row per code. Each row has five fields:

the concept (for example cryptococcosis or lumbar_puncture);
the code type: diagnosis, procedure or HCPCS;
the code system;
the code, without its decimal point;
whether the code matches exactly or as a prefix;
its source: the reconstruction, or the supplement for the HCPCS codes.

Every code matches exactly, except the diabetes stems. The reconstruction listed each diabetes stem alone or followed by one or two digits, which misses most ICD-10-CM diabetes codes (for example E11649). So the stems match as open prefixes, as in the supplement: E11 matches E1122 and E11649 alike. ICD-9-CM 456.20 (esophageal varices with bleeding, in diseases classified elsewhere) is added to cirrhosis; both sources list only its counterpart 456.21. The cyclosporine and tacrolimus HCPCS codes appear only in the supplement. Immunosuppression is measured from the UNOS records instead (#2), so they are not used, but they are kept, marked, in case billing data are revisited as the source. The reconstruction also has an IRIS list and a principal-diagnosis cryptococcosis list, which the paper’s analyses do not use and which are left out.
The paper reports ventriculoperitoneal shunt placement, but neither the supplement nor the reconstruction lists its codes, which the maintainer judged a copy/paste loss. The list is rebuilt from the official code sets: ICD-9-CM 02.34 and the nine ICD-10-PCS “Bypass Cerebral Ventricle to Peritoneal Cavity” codes. All ten are also in the neurosurgical list. That includes the three-character B45 in the cryptococcosis list, which therefore matches only a code recorded as B45 itself.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Diabetes stems as open prefixes, as Supplementary Table 1 lists them (250*,
# E08*, E09*, E10*, E11*, E13*), so every subcode matches, including 6- and
# 7-character ICD-10-CM codes such as E11649. The reconstruction's version
# stopped at two extra digits and missed most ICD-10 diabetes codes.
diabetes_prefix_codes <- tibble(
  concept = "diabetes",
  code_type = "diagnosis",
  code_system = c("ICD-9-CM", rep("ICD-10-CM", 5)),
  code = c("250", "E08", "E09", "E10", "E11", "E13"),
  match = "prefix",
  source = "supplement"
)

title: Code lists
text:
Ventriculoperitoneal shunt
The VP shunt codes, rebuilt from the official code sets because neither source lists them (see above). Shunt replacement and removal are not placement and are left out.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Ventriculoperitoneal shunt placement: ICD-9-CM 02.34 "Ventricular shunt to
# abdominal cavity and organs"; ICD-10-PCS "Bypass Cerebral Ventricle to
# Peritoneal Cavity" with autologous (7), synthetic (J) or nonautologous (K)
# substitute, by open (0), percutaneous (3) or percutaneous endoscopic (4)
# approach. Shunt replacement (02.42) and removal (02.43) are not placement
# and are excluded.
vp_shunt_codes <- expand_grid(
  approach = c("0", "3", "4"),
  device = c("7", "J", "K")
) %>%
  transmute(
    code = str_c("0016", approach, device, "6"),
    code_system = "ICD-10-PCS"
  ) %>%
  add_row(code = "0234", code_system = "ICD-9-CM") %>%
  mutate(
    concept = "vp_shunt",
    code_type = "procedure",
    match = "exact",
    source = "official code sets (missing from both lists)"
  )

code_lists <- code_lists %>%
  bind_rows(diabetes_prefix_codes, cirrhosis_addition_codes, vp_shunt_codes) %>%
  mutate(
    source = case_when(
      code_type == "hcpcs" ~ "supplement (not used; issue #2)",
      .default = source
    )
  )

Immunosuppressive drug classes
UNOS records each immunosuppressive drug by a numeric code (RX_CD), with free text when the drug is “other”. This table assigns each code to one of the classes the paper reports. The free-text table keeps the reconstruction’s spellings, including the misspellings found in the data.

title: Survival and models
text: This script fits the survival curve and the logistic models for 6-month mortality, following plan §8. Tables and figures are made from these results in a separate step.

title: Survival and models
text:
Survival curve
A Kaplan–Meier estimate of survival from the index admission (Figure 2).


Click to show/hide R Code
# Kaplan-Meier estimate of survival from the index admission (Figure 2).
km_fit <- survfit(
  Surv(survival_days, survival_event) ~ 1,
  data = analysis_data
)

title: Survival and models
text:
Each variable alone
Every candidate variable is tested on its own, using everyone whose value is known.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Each candidate alone, on the people with it known.
bivariable_results <- bivariable_models(
  model_data,
  outcome = "died_within_window",
  candidates = model_candidates
)

title: Survival and models
text:
Multivariable model
All candidates go in together. The variable with the largest P value is then removed, one at a time, until every remaining variable has P below 0.05. The paper gave no threshold for entry and kept no variable in by force. The model uses everyone with every candidate known, and the number left out is reported.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Every candidate entered, then backward elimination at P < .05, on the
# complete cases for all candidates (plan §8).
multivariable <- backward_eliminate(
  model_data,
  outcome = "died_within_window",
  candidates = model_candidates,
  threshold = elimination_threshold
)

title: Survival and models
text:
The paper’s final model
The paper’s eight-variable final model is also fitted exactly as published, on the same people as the backward elimination. Its odds ratios can then be compared with the published ones directly, whether or not the selection here keeps the same eight variables.
The two approaches answer different questions. Rerunning the selection asks whether the paper’s method, applied to this data release, picks the same characteristics; selection by P value is unstable, so it may not, even when nothing is wrong. Refitting the published model asks whether the same characteristics have similar odds ratios here. The Study design and methods page sets out these and the other choices in how the model is built.


Click to show/hide R Code
# The paper's final model, fitted as published: its eight terms on the same
# people as the backward elimination (complete cases for every candidate),
# because the paper's estimates come from the end of that selection
# (plan §8). Compared with the published odds ratios in Table 4.
published_fit <- glm(
  reformulate(published_model$term, response = "died_within_window"),
  family = binomial(),
  data = multivariable$data
)

title: Survival and models
text:
Goodness of fit
The Hosmer–Lemeshow test compares predicted with observed deaths across tenths of predicted risk.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Hosmer-Lemeshow goodness of fit of the final model, with deciles of risk.
hosmer_lemeshow_result <- hosmer_lemeshow(
  observed = multivariable$data$died_within_window,
  predicted = fitted(multivariable$model)
)

title: Data sources
text: This page describes where the study’s data come from and what they can and cannot show. Which files each step uses is on the Study design and methods page and in the usRds coverage assessment.

title: Data sources
section: The United States Renal Data System
text:
The United States Renal Data System
The United States Renal Data System (USRDS) is the national data system for chronic kidney disease and end-stage kidney disease in the United States, run for the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases. It links registry information on almost everyone treated for kidney failure with their Medicare billing records and with transplant records from the Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network (OPTN)1,2. The published supplement shows its sources in a diagram.
Its strengths are near-complete coverage of people with kidney failure in the United States and the link to Medicare claims; its limits include that its methods are not continuously validated2. Billing records are released only for people with Medicare fee-for-service coverage: USRDS receives claims for people in Medicare Advantage plans but does not release them in its standard files1. Care paid by other insurers, or by Medicare Advantage plans, is therefore not seen.

title: Data sources
text:
The files this study uses

Hospitalization files. Records of hospital stays paid by Medicare, with their diagnosis and procedure codes1: up to 10 diagnosis codes in the file for stays before 2010 (hosp_to2009), and up to 26 in the later file (hosp_2010on). A long stay can be billed in more than one record, and the analysis combines them. The study’s cases, the index hospitalization and the conditions during it come from these files.
Physician and supplier claims. Bills from physicians and other providers, with their diagnosis codes. The study uses them to find cryptococcosis before transplant.
Patient and transplant files. Date of birth, sex, race, ethnicity, state of residence and date of death, and the date of every kidney transplant and graft failure.
OPTN transplant records. The registration at each transplant, the follow-up reports after it, and the immunosuppressive drugs recorded at transplant and at follow-up1. These give body mass index, dialysis before transplant, HIV and cytomegalovirus status, rejection and the drugs in Table 2.

The extract used here begins on 1 January 2006, the start of the study period; there are no earlier records.

title: Data sources
text:
Diagnosis codes
Diagnoses and procedures are coded in the International Classification of Diseases. US claims switched from the 9th revision (ICD-9-CM) to the 10th (ICD-10-CM for diagnoses, ICD-10-PCS for inpatient procedures) on 1 October 20153, so the study period has nearly ten years of ICD-9 coding and fifteen months of ICD-10. Every code list therefore has both versions; the lists are on the Code lists page.
A diagnosis in a claim means a provider billed for it, not that it was confirmed. No study was found that measures how accurately billing codes identify cryptococcosis in Medicare or USRDS data. The nearest evidence concerns other infections. In transplant recipients at one hospital, the ICD-9 code for invasive aspergillosis found 63% of confirmed cases, and 71% of the patients it flagged had the infection4. Codes for cytomegalovirus after kidney transplant performed similarly in another centre5, and codes for invasive fungal infection moderately well in children with cancer6. Which kind of accuracy matters depends on the use: excluding people with an earlier condition calls for a high negative predictive value, so that few of the people kept had the condition, and defining a cohort calls for a high positive predictive value, so that few of the people included lack it7.

title: Data sources
text:
Access and disclosure
USRDS data are released only under a data use agreement. Results may not be published if any table cell, or any number that can be worked out from others, describes fewer than 11 people8. This is why counts from 1 to 10 are hidden in this project’s tables and figures, and why nothing on this site comes from the data. The data are read through the usRds package, on a machine with authorized access.

title: Building the cohort
text: This script builds the study cohort: one row per person, each with their index cryptococcosis hospitalization. It follows the steps in §4 of the analysis plan, and every exclusion goes through the cohort flowchart (Figure 1).

title: Building the cohort
text:
Loading the hospitalization files
The cohort starts from the two USRDS hospitalization files, which hold Medicare inpatient stays (decided in #1). Only the dates and diagnosis columns are loaded.
Factor labels are switched off, so codes stay as plain text. usRds has no function that searches these files for codes, so each file is loaded whole and searched by the project’s own code. The usRds coverage page records this as a gap (step 4).


Click to show/hide R Code
# Columns are chosen with select() after loading, not with col_select,
# because load_usrds_file() fails on Parquet files when col_select is used
# (usRds#22). Return to col_select once that is fixed.
# Both hospitalization files, with the key fields and diagnosis columns only.
# factor_labels = FALSE keeps diagnosis codes as character (in hosp_to2009,
# PRIMDIAG is a Y/N flag that Appendix C would otherwise turn into a factor).
# usRds gap (coverage map, step 4): no extractor for these files, so each is
# loaded whole and searched here.
hosp_to2009 <- load_usrds_file(
  "hosp_to2009",
  factor_labels = FALSE
) %>%
  select(all_of(c("USRDS_ID", "CLM_FROM", "CLM_THRU", hosp_to2009_dx_columns)))
hosp_2010on <- load_usrds_file(
  "hosp_2010on",
  factor_labels = FALSE
) %>%
  select(all_of(c("USRDS_ID", "CLM_FROM", "CLM_THRU", hosp_2010on_dx_columns)))

title: Building the cohort
text:
Flagging cryptococcosis
Each record is flagged if any of its diagnosis columns holds a cryptococcosis code from the code lists. The search uses each file’s own diagnosis columns.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Flag cryptococcosis on every hospitalization record, using each file's own
# diagnosis columns.
cryptococcosis_codes <- codes_for_concept(code_lists, "cryptococcosis")

hosp_records <- bind_rows(
  flag_cryptococcosis_records(hosp_to2009, hosp_to2009_dx_columns, cryptococcosis_codes),
  flag_cryptococcosis_records(hosp_2010on, hosp_2010on_dx_columns, cryptococcosis_codes)
)

rm(hosp_to2009, hosp_2010on)

title: Building the cohort
text:
Building stays
For people with any cryptococcosis record, all their hospitalization records are combined into stays, so a code on any record of a stay counts for the whole stay. Stays admitted from 2006 to 2016 are kept.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Combine all hospitalization records of people with any cryptococcosis
# record into stays, so a cryptococcosis code on any record of an overlapping
# stay counts for the whole stay (plan §5). Keep stays admitted in the window.
people_with_cryptococcosis <- hosp_records %>%
  filter(cryptococcosis_record) %>%
  distinct(USRDS_ID)

cryptococcosis_stays <- hosp_records %>%
  semi_join(people_with_cryptococcosis, by = "USRDS_ID") %>%
  summarise_cryptococcosis_stays(study_start_date, study_end_date)

# Every cryptococcosis hospital record, of any year, for the prior-claim
# exclusion below
hospital_cryptococcosis_claims <- hosp_records %>%
  filter(cryptococcosis_record) %>%
  select(USRDS_ID, claim_date = CLM_FROM)

rm(hosp_records)

title: Building the cohort
text:
Transplant and birth dates
Each person’s first transplant date comes from the USRDS transplant file, and their date of birth from the patients file. Both are loaded only for the people found above.


Click to show/hide R Code
# First transplant date from the transplant file; date of birth from the
# patients file. Only the people with a cryptococcosis stay are kept.
first_transplants <- load_usrds_file(
  "tx",
  usrds_ids = cryptococcosis_stays$USRDS_ID
) %>%
  select(all_of(c("USRDS_ID", "TDATE"))) %>%
  first_transplant_dates()

patients <- load_usrds_file(
  "patients",
  usrds_ids = cryptococcosis_stays$USRDS_ID
) %>%
  select(all_of(c("USRDS_ID", "BORN")))

title: Building the cohort
text:
Physician claims
The paper excludes anyone with a cryptococcosis claim, “physician or hospitalization”, before their first transplant. Hospital records are already loaded; physician and supplier claims come from usRds::get_PS_ICD(), for the people with a cryptococcosis stay, searched for the same cryptococcosis codes. That function matches codes exactly, so the run stops if the code list ever gains a prefix code that it would miss.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Physician/supplier claims with a cryptococcosis code, for the people with a
# cryptococcosis stay (plan §4, step 4). usRds::get_PS_ICD() matches exact
# codes, which the cryptococcosis list is. Covered by usRds (coverage map,
# step 10). A prefix code would be silently missed, so the run stops if the
# list ever gains one.
stopifnot(all(cryptococcosis_codes$match == "exact"))

physician_cryptococcosis_claims <- get_PS_ICD(
  icd_codes = cryptococcosis_codes$code,
  years = physician_claim_years,
  usrds_ids = cryptococcosis_stays$USRDS_ID
) %>%
  select(USRDS_ID, claim_date = CLM_FROM)

title: Building the cohort
text:
Cohort candidates
One row per person, with their index stay and age. A single cryptococcosis claim of either kind, dated before the person’s first transplant, marks them for exclusion (#4). One claim is enough: a clinician billing for cryptococcosis, even to rule it out, before transplant is a reason to doubt that the later episode is new, and studies that exclude an earlier condition usually take any single claim, because missing an earlier case matters more there than excluding a few people over a rule-out code1.


Click to show/hide R Code
# One cryptococcosis claim of either kind before the first transplant
# excludes the person (decided under issue #4).
prior_cryptococcosis <- prior_cryptococcosis_ids(
  bind_rows(hospital_cryptococcosis_claims, physician_cryptococcosis_claims),
  first_transplants
)

cohort_candidates <- build_cohort_candidates(
  cryptococcosis_stays,
  first_transplants,
  patients
) %>%
  mutate(no_prior_cryptococcosis = !USRDS_ID %in% prior_cryptococcosis)

title: Building the cohort
text:
Flowchart
The exclusions are applied in the plan’s order, each as a flowchart step, so Figure 1 shows exactly how the cohort was reached:

people in the transplant file;
people with a cryptococcosis stay admitted on or after their first transplant (a stay admitted before it counts as cryptococcosis before transplant, which the paper excludes);
people with no cryptococcosis claim, hospital or physician, before their first transplant;
people aged 18 to 90 at index admission.

The box labels are built from the study constants, so they can’t fall out of step with the window or age range. The flowchart’s final data is the cohort.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Every exclusion goes through fc_filter(), so Figure 1 reproduces the cohort
# exactly. Box labels are built from the constants in setup.R.
cohort_flowchart <- cohort_candidates %>%
  as_fc(
    label = str_glue(
      "People with a cryptococcosis hospitalization admitted ",
      "{format(study_start_date, '%Y')}-{format(study_end_date, '%Y')}"
    )
  ) %>%
  fc_filter(
    in_transplant_file,
    label = "In the USRDS transplant file",
    show_exc = TRUE
  ) %>%
  fc_filter(
    !is.na(index_stay_id),
    label = "Cryptococcosis hospitalization admitted on or after first transplant",
    show_exc = TRUE
  ) %>%
  fc_filter(
    no_prior_cryptococcosis,
    label = "No cryptococcosis claim (hospital or physician) before first transplant",
    show_exc = TRUE
  ) %>%
  fc_filter(
    between(age_at_index, age_min, age_max),
    label = str_glue("Aged {age_min}-{age_max} years at index admission"),
    show_exc = TRUE
  )

cohort <- flowchart::fc_view(cohort_flowchart, what = "data")

title: Building the cohort
text:
Variable labels
The derived variables get human-readable labels.


Click to show/hide R Code
cohort <- cohort %>%
  set_variable_labels(
    first_transplant_date = "Date of first transplant (USRDS transplant file)",
    in_transplant_file = "Has a record in the USRDS transplant file",
    index_stay_id = "Index cryptococcosis stay (person and stay number)",
    index_admit_date = "Admission date of the index stay (time zero)",
    index_discharge_date = "Discharge date of the index stay",
    age_at_index = "Age at index admission (completed years)",
    no_prior_cryptococcosis = "No cryptococcosis claim (hospital or physician/supplier) before first transplant"
  )

title: Outcomes
text:
PendingProvisional



Text highlighted like this is provisional: it depends on a decision the analysis plan has not yet made.
This script adds the mortality outcomes (plan §7) and puts the variables in the form the model uses (plan §8).

title: Outcomes
text:
Dates of death
Dates of death come from the USRDS patients file. Each person needs only one row, because every characteristic is fixed at the start and death is the only event. That is why the usRds cohort functions aren’t used here; the coverage assessment records what testing them showed.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Columns are chosen with select() after loading, not with col_select,
# because load_usrds_file() fails on Parquet files when col_select is used
# (usRds#22). Return to col_select once that is fixed.
# Date of death from the patients file. The usRds cohort functions are not
# used: every covariate is fixed and death is the only event, so one row per
# person is enough (coverage map, step 18).
deaths <- load_usrds_file(
  "patients",
  usrds_ids = analysis_data$USRDS_ID,
  factor_labels = FALSE
) %>%
  select(all_of(c("USRDS_ID", "DIED")))

title: Outcomes
text:
Mortality
The script adds three things for each person:

death within 180 days of the index admission, where deaths on the admission day and on day 180 both count;
days to death;
for the survival curve, time to death or to the end of the release’s death data.


Decision pending: the end of the death data (death_data_end_date) has to be set for the release in use. The script stops until it is.



Click to show/hide R Code
mortality <- six_month_outcomes(
  analysis_data,
  deaths,
  window_days = mortality_window_days,
  data_end_date = death_data_end_date
)

analysis_data <- analysis_data %>%
  left_join(mortality, by = "USRDS_ID", relationship = "one-to-one")

stopifnot(nrow(analysis_data) == nrow(cohort))

title: Outcomes
text:
Model variables
The model uses the forms the paper reports:

age 60 or older;
more than one transplant;
any graft failure;
not being on tacrolimus.



Click to show/hide R Code
# Variables in the form the paper's model reports them: age 60 or older, more
# than one transplant, any graft failure, and not being on tacrolimus.
# Categories are in the paper's Table 1 order, and the first is the
# reference: Female, White, West. The paper shows Hispanic ethnicity as one
# yes row, so non-Hispanic is the reference; for organ and serostatus, the
# usual category (kidney alone, negative). The paper does not name its
# reference categories; every term in its final model is yes or no.
model_data <- analysis_data %>%
  mutate(
    age_60_or_older = age_at_index >= age_model_cutoff,
    more_than_one_transplant = transplants_before_index > 1,
    prior_graft_failure = failures_before_index > 0,
    no_tacrolimus_at_transplant = !tx_tacrolimus,
    no_tacrolimus_at_followup = !fu_tacrolimus,
    sex = factor(sex, levels = c("Female", "Male")),
    race = factor(race, levels = c("White", "Black", "Other")),
    hispanic = factor(hispanic, levels = c("Non-Hispanic", "Hispanic")),
    region = factor(region, levels = c("West", "Midwest", "South", "Northeast", "Outside")),
    organ = factor(organ, levels = c("Kidney", "Kidney-pancreas")),
    hiv_status = factor(hiv_status, levels = c("Negative", "Positive")),
    cmv_status = factor(cmv_status, levels = c("Negative", "Positive"))
  )
# A value outside the listed categories would silently become missing
for (variable in c("sex", "race", "hispanic", "region", "organ", "hiv_status", "cmv_status")) {
  stopifnot(sum(is.na(model_data[[variable]])) == sum(is.na(analysis_data[[variable]])))
}

title: Outcomes
text:
Labels


Click to show/hide R Code
analysis_data <- analysis_data %>%
  set_variable_labels(
    days_to_death = "Days from index admission to death",
    died_within_window = str_glue("Died within {mortality_window_days} days of index admission"),
    survival_days = "Days from index admission to death or end of death data",
    survival_event = "Died before the end of death data (1) or censored (0)"
  )

title: Functions
text: This script defines the helper functions the analysis scripts share. Three of them do work that usRds does not yet do, and are labelled “usRds gap” in the code. The coverage assessment explains each gap.

title: Functions
Functions
text:
Matching codes
code_matches() compares a vector of recorded codes with a code list. It handles both exact codes and prefixes, so the diabetes stems match all their subcodes. The usRds get_*_ICD() functions match exactly only, which is why this exists (coverage step 6).


Click to show/hide R Code
# usRds gap (coverage map, step 6): the get_*_ICD() functions match codes
# exactly; this also handles prefix matching ("250" matches "25000").
# Returns TRUE where a code in `values` matches any code in `codes`.
code_matches <- function(values, codes) {
  exact_codes <- codes %>%
    filter(match == "exact") %>%
    pull(code)
  prefix_codes <- codes %>%
    filter(match == "prefix") %>%
    pull(code)

  matched <- !is.na(values) & values %in% exact_codes
  for (prefix in prefix_codes) {
    matched <- matched | (!is.na(values) & str_starts(values, fixed(prefix)))
  }
  matched
}

title: Functions
Functions
text:
Combining records into stays
A single hospital stay can appear as several hospitalization records. collapse_stays() puts a person’s records in date order. It starts a new stay only when a record’s admission date falls after the latest discharge date seen so far, so the stays it builds never overlap. A record admitted on the day of the previous discharge joins the same stay. The optional gap_days argument also joins records that start within that many days of discharge.
The function adds a stay identifier and the stay’s first and last dates. The plan treats overlapping or contiguous records as one stay (§5); usRds has no equivalent (coverage step 7).


Click to show/hide R Code
# usRds gap (coverage map, step 7): hospitalization records whose admission
# date falls on or before the latest discharge date so far for the same person
# (plus `gap_days`) belong to the same stay. Adds stay_id (unique across
# people), stay_from and stay_thru. Input needs USRDS_ID, CLM_FROM, CLM_THRU.
collapse_stays <- function(records, gap_days = 0) {
  records %>%
    arrange(USRDS_ID, CLM_FROM, CLM_THRU) %>%
    group_by(USRDS_ID) %>%
    mutate(
      latest_thru_before = lag(cummax(as.numeric(CLM_THRU))),
      starts_new_stay = case_when(
        is.na(latest_thru_before) ~ TRUE,
        as.numeric(CLM_FROM) > latest_thru_before + gap_days ~ TRUE,
        .default = FALSE
      ),
      stay_number = cumsum(starts_new_stay)
    ) %>%
    group_by(USRDS_ID, stay_number) %>%
    mutate(
      stay_from = min(CLM_FROM),
      stay_thru = max(CLM_THRU)
    ) %>%
    ungroup() %>%
    mutate(stay_id = str_c(USRDS_ID, "-", stay_number)) %>%
    select(-latest_thru_before, -starts_new_stay, -stay_number)
}

title: Functions
text:
Age in years
age_in_years() gives age at last birthday on a given date, so a person is 18 on their 18th birthday. The plan’s age range, 18 to 90 years, is applied to this.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Completed years of age on a date (age at last birthday).
age_in_years <- function(born, on) {
  floor(time_length(interval(born, on), unit = "years"))
}

title: Functions
text:
First transplant date
first_transplant_dates() reduces the transplant file, which has one row per transplant, to each person’s earliest transplant date. Rows without a date are ignored.


Click to show/hide R Code
# One row per person: the date of their first transplant in the USRDS
# transplant file. Input needs USRDS_ID and TDATE.
first_transplant_dates <- function(transplants) {
  transplants %>%
    filter(!is.na(TDATE)) %>%
    group_by(USRDS_ID) %>%
    summarise(first_transplant_date = min(TDATE), .groups = "drop")
}

title: Functions
text:
Flagging cryptococcosis records
flag_cryptococcosis_records() marks each hospitalization record that has a cryptococcosis code in any diagnosis column. It’s told which columns to search, because the two hospitalization files differ (see Setup).


Click to show/hide R Code
# Keep each hospitalization record's key fields and flag whether any of its
# diagnosis columns holds a cryptococcosis code. `dx_columns` differs by file
# (see setup.R).
flag_cryptococcosis_records <- function(records, dx_columns, crypto_codes) {
  records %>%
    mutate(
      cryptococcosis_record = flag_codes_wide(records, dx_columns, crypto_codes)
    ) %>%
    select(USRDS_ID, CLM_FROM, CLM_THRU, cryptococcosis_record)
}

title: Functions
text:
Cryptococcosis stays
summarise_cryptococcosis_stays() combines a person’s records into stays with collapse_stays(). A stay counts as a cryptococcosis stay if any of its records has the code. The function keeps stays admitted within the study window, with both boundary dates included.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Combine records into stays (collapse_stays()) and keep the stays with a
# cryptococcosis code on any of their records, admitted in the study window.
# Returns one row per stay: USRDS_ID, stay_id, stay_from, stay_thru.
summarise_cryptococcosis_stays <- function(records, window_start, window_end) {
  records %>%
    collapse_stays() %>%
    group_by(USRDS_ID, stay_id, stay_from, stay_thru) %>%
    summarise(
      cryptococcosis_stay = any(cryptococcosis_record),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) %>%
    filter(
      cryptococcosis_stay,
      stay_from >= window_start,
      stay_from <= window_end
    ) %>%
    select(-cryptococcosis_stay)
}

title: Functions
text:
Cohort candidates
build_cohort_candidates() makes one row per person with a cryptococcosis stay in the window. It adds the facts the cohort flowchart filters on:

whether the person is in the transplant file;
their index stay: the first cryptococcosis stay admitted on or after their first transplant;
their age on the index admission date.

A stay admitted on the day of the first transplant counts; a stay admitted the day before does not, even if it continues past the transplant. The function excludes no one itself; the exclusions happen in the flowchart.


Click to show/hide R Code
# One row per person with at least one cryptococcosis stay in the window,
# with the flags the cohort flowchart filters on (plan §4):
#   in_transplant_file: has a record in the USRDS transplant file;
#   index_stay_id, index_admit_date, index_discharge_date: the first
#     cryptococcosis stay admitted on or after the first transplant (NA when
#     there is none). A stay admitted before the first transplant is a
#     cryptococcosis hospitalization claim preceding it, which the paper
#     excludes (decided under issue #4);
#   age_at_index: completed years on the index admission date.
build_cohort_candidates <- function(crypto_stays, first_transplants, patients) {
  index_stays <- crypto_stays %>%
    inner_join(first_transplants, by = "USRDS_ID", relationship = "many-to-one") %>%
    filter(stay_from >= first_transplant_date) %>%
    group_by(USRDS_ID) %>%
    slice_min(stay_from, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
    ungroup() %>%
    select(
      USRDS_ID,
      index_stay_id = stay_id,
      index_admit_date = stay_from,
      index_discharge_date = stay_thru
    )

  crypto_stays %>%
    distinct(USRDS_ID) %>%
    left_join(first_transplants, by = "USRDS_ID", relationship = "one-to-one") %>%
    mutate(in_transplant_file = !is.na(first_transplant_date)) %>%
    left_join(index_stays, by = "USRDS_ID", relationship = "one-to-one") %>%
    left_join(
      patients %>% select(USRDS_ID, BORN),
      by = "USRDS_ID",
      relationship = "one-to-one"
    ) %>%
    mutate(age_at_index = age_in_years(BORN, index_admit_date)) %>%
    select(-BORN)
}


prior_cryptococcosis_ids() takes every cryptococcosis claim (hospital records and physician claims together, one row per claim with its first day of service) and returns the people with any claim before their first transplant. A claim on the transplant date itself does not count as before it, the same rule as for hospital stays.


Click to show/hide R Code
# People with any cryptococcosis claim before their first transplant (plan
# §4, step 4; decided under issue #4: hospital and physician/supplier claims
# both count, and one claim is enough). `claims` has one row per claim:
# USRDS_ID and claim_date (the first day of service). A claim on the
# transplant date itself is not before it, matching the rule for hospital
# stays. Returns the USRDS_IDs to exclude.
prior_cryptococcosis_ids <- function(claims, first_transplants) {
  claims %>%
    inner_join(first_transplants, by = "USRDS_ID", relationship = "many-to-one") %>%
    filter(claim_date < first_transplant_date) %>%
    distinct(USRDS_ID) %>%
    pull(USRDS_ID)
}

title: Functions
Functions
text:
Loading and flagging hospitalizations
load_flagged_hospitalizations() loads one hospitalization file for a set of people through usRds. It flags the diagnosis and procedure concepts on each record, and keeps the dates, ICU and CCU days, and the flags.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Load one hospitalization file for a set of people (usRds::load_usrds_file())
# and flag diagnosis and procedure concepts on each record, keeping the key
# fields, ICU/CCU days and the flags. Codes stay character
# (factor_labels = FALSE). Columns are selected after loading because of
# usRds#22. usRds gap (coverage map, steps 4-9).
load_flagged_hospitalizations <- function(file_root, ids, dx_columns, proc_columns,
                                          dx_concepts, proc_concepts, code_lists) {
  key_columns <- c("USRDS_ID", "CLM_FROM", "CLM_THRU", "ICU_DAYS", "CCU_DAYS")

  load_usrds_file(
    file_root,
    factor_labels = FALSE,
    usrds_ids = ids
  ) %>%
    select(all_of(c(key_columns, dx_columns, proc_columns))) %>%
    flag_concepts(dx_columns, code_lists, dx_concepts) %>%
    flag_concepts(proc_columns, code_lists, proc_concepts) %>%
    select(all_of(c(key_columns, dx_concepts, proc_concepts)))
}

title: Functions
text:
Index stay covariates
summarise_index_stay() takes the records that fall within each person’s index stay, meaning those admitted between the stay’s first and last dates. A concept counts if any of those records has it. ICU admission means any ICU or CCU days on the stay.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Stay-level covariates for the index stay. A record belongs to the index stay
# when it is admitted within the stay's span (true of every record that
# collapse_stays() combined into it). Returns one row per person: each
# concept flag (TRUE if any record of the stay has it) and icu_admission
# (any ICU or CCU days on the stay).
summarise_index_stay <- function(records, cohort_index, concepts) {
  records %>%
    inner_join(
      cohort_index %>% select(USRDS_ID, index_admit_date, index_discharge_date),
      by = "USRDS_ID",
      relationship = "many-to-one"
    ) %>%
    filter(
      CLM_FROM >= index_admit_date,
      CLM_FROM <= index_discharge_date
    ) %>%
    group_by(USRDS_ID) %>%
    summarise(
      across(all_of(concepts), any),
      icu_days = sum(coalesce(ICU_DAYS, 0) + coalesce(CCU_DAYS, 0)),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) %>%
    mutate(icu_admission = icu_days > 0) %>%
    select(-icu_days)
}

title: Functions
text:
Earlier hospitalizations
summarise_prior_hospitalizations() reports whether any hospitalization admitted before the index admission carries a given flag, such as a transplant-complication code. People with no earlier hospitalizations get “no”.

# TRUE when any hospitalization record admitted before the index admission has
# `flag_column` set (for example, a transplant-complication code).
summarise_prior_hospitalizations <- function(records, cohort_index, flag_column) {

    inner_join(
      cohort_index %>% select(USRDS_ID, index_admit_date),
      by = "USRDS_ID",
      relationship = "many-to-one"
    ) %>%
    filter(CLM_FROM < index_admit_date) %>%
    group_by(USRDS_ID) %>%
    summarise(prior = any(.data[[flag_column]]), .groups = "drop")

    select(USRDS_ID) %>%
    left_join(prior, by = "USRDS_ID", relationship = "one-to-one") %>%
    mutate(prior = coalesce(prior, FALSE))

title: Functions
text:
Transplant history
summarise_transplant_history() takes everyone’s transplants and, for each person, counts:

transplants on or before the index admission;
graft failures before it;
the days since the most recent transplant.



Click to show/hide R Code
# Transplant history at the index admission, from the USRDS transplant file
# (one row per transplant; needs USRDS_ID, TDATE, FAILDATE):
#   transplants_before_index: transplants dated on or before index admission;
#   failures_before_index: graft failures dated before index admission;
#   last_transplant_date, days_since_last_transplant: most recent transplant
#     on or before index admission.
summarise_transplant_history <- function(transplants, cohort_index) {
  transplants %>%
    inner_join(
      cohort_index %>% select(USRDS_ID, index_admit_date),
      by = "USRDS_ID",
      relationship = "many-to-one"
    ) %>%
    filter(!is.na(TDATE), TDATE <= index_admit_date) %>%
    group_by(USRDS_ID) %>%
    summarise(
      transplants_before_index = n(),
      failures_before_index = sum(!is.na(FAILDATE) & FAILDATE < index_admit_date),
      last_transplant_date = max(TDATE),
      days_since_last_transplant = as.numeric(first(index_admit_date) - max(TDATE)),
      .groups = "drop"
    )
}

title: Functions
text:
Acute rejection
unos_rejection_any() turns the UNOS rejection code into yes or no. Codes 1 and 2 (an episode, treated or not) are “yes”, and 3 is “no”. Unknown codes are missing.


Click to show/hide R Code
# UNOS acute rejection (format ACREJEPI): 1 (treated) or 2 (not treated with
# an additional agent) is an episode; 3 is none; blank, 990 and 998 (unknown)
# are missing (decided 2026-11-10).
unos_rejection_any <- function(code) {
  code <- as.character(code)
  case_when(
    code %in% c("1", "2") ~ TRUE,
    code == "3" ~ FALSE,
    .default = NA
  )
}

title: Functions
text:
Drug classes
classify_immunosuppressants() gives one row per registration or follow-up, with a yes/no column per drug class. A class is “yes” when any drug record maps to it, by code or by free text.


Click to show/hide R Code
# One row per key with one logical column per drug class: TRUE when any of the
# key's drug records maps to the class, by drug code (RX_CD) or by free text
# (DRUG_CD_OSTXT). Keys with no records are absent; callers decide whether
# absence means "not on" or missing.
classify_immunosuppressants <- function(drug_records, key, rx_classes, free_text) {
  by_code <- drug_records %>%
    inner_join(
      rx_classes %>% select(rx_cd, drug_class),
      by = c("RX_CD" = "rx_cd"),
      relationship = "many-to-one"
    )
  by_text <- drug_records %>%
    inner_join(
      free_text,
      by = c("DRUG_CD_OSTXT" = "drug_text"),
      relationship = "many-to-one"
    )
  all_classes <- sort(unique(rx_classes$drug_class))

  bind_rows(by_code, by_text) %>%
    distinct(.data[[key]], drug_class) %>%
    mutate(on_drug = TRUE, drug_class = factor(drug_class, levels = all_classes)) %>%
    pivot_wider(
      names_from = drug_class,
      values_from = on_drug,
      values_fill = FALSE,
      names_expand = TRUE
    ) %>%
    right_join(distinct(drug_records, .data[[key]]), by = key) %>%
    mutate(across(all_of(all_classes), \(x) coalesce(x, FALSE)))
}

title: Functions
Functions
text:
Combining yes/no values
any_known() combines several yes/no values while keeping missing distinct from “no”. The result is “yes” if any value is yes, “no” if none is yes and at least one is no, and missing if every value is missing.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Combine logical values, keeping missing distinct from "no": TRUE if any value
# is TRUE; FALSE if none is TRUE and at least one is FALSE; NA if all are
# missing (or there are none).
any_known <- function(x) {
  case_when(
    any(x %in% TRUE) ~ TRUE,
    any(x %in% FALSE) ~ FALSE,
    .default = NA
  )
}

title: Functions
text:
Mortality outcomes
six_month_outcomes() counts days from the index admission to death, with the admission day as day 0, and flags death within the 180-day window. Deaths on day 180, and on the admission day itself, both count. For the survival curve, people still alive are followed to the end of the release’s death data. The function stops if that date hasn’t been set.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Mortality outcomes from the index admission (plan §7): days to death;
# died_within_window (death on or before day `window_days`, with the
# admission day as day 0); and survival time and event for Kaplan-Meier,
# censored at `data_end_date`. A death on the admission day has time 0.
# `deaths` needs USRDS_ID and DIED (missing if alive).
six_month_outcomes <- function(cohort_index, deaths, window_days, data_end_date) {
  if (is.na(data_end_date)) {
    stop(
      "death_data_end_date must be set in R/setup.R for the USRDS release in use.",
      call. = FALSE
    )
  }

  cohort_index %>%
    select(USRDS_ID, index_admit_date) %>%
    left_join(deaths %>% select(USRDS_ID, DIED), by = "USRDS_ID", relationship = "one-to-one") %>%
    mutate(
      death_observed = !is.na(DIED) & DIED <= data_end_date,
      days_to_death = if_else(death_observed, as.numeric(DIED - index_admit_date), NA),
      died_within_window = death_observed & days_to_death <= window_days,
      survival_days = if_else(
        death_observed,
        days_to_death,
        as.numeric(data_end_date - index_admit_date)
      ),
      survival_event = as.integer(death_observed)
    ) %>%
    select(-DIED, -index_admit_date, -death_observed)
}

title: Functions
text:
One P value per variable
wald_term_p() tests all of a variable’s coefficients together. A variable with several categories, such as region, therefore gets one P value, as in Stata’s stepwise procedure, which the paper used.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Joint Wald test P value for one term of a fitted glm (all its coefficients
# together, so a factor gets one P value), as Stata's stepwise uses by
# default.
wald_term_p <- function(model, term) {
  term_index <- match(term, attr(terms(model), "term.labels"))
  columns <- which(attr(model.matrix(model), "assign") == term_index)
  estimates <- coef(model)[columns]
  keep <- !is.na(estimates)
  estimates <- estimates[keep]
  if (length(estimates) == 0) {
    # No estimable coefficient (the term does not vary in the sample)
    return(NA_real_)
  }
  covariance <- vcov(model)[names(estimates), names(estimates), drop = FALSE]
  statistic <- as.numeric(t(estimates) %*% solve(covariance) %*% estimates)
  pchisq(statistic, df = length(estimates), lower.tail = FALSE)
}

title: Functions
text:
Bivariable models
bivariable_models() fits one logistic model per candidate variable. Each model uses everyone whose value of that variable is known.


Click to show/hide R Code
# One logistic model per candidate (outcome ~ candidate), each on the people
# with that candidate known. Returns the term, people used, and Wald P value
# (NA when the candidate does not vary among them).
bivariable_models <- function(data, outcome, candidates) {
  map(candidates, \(candidate) {
    model_data <- data %>%
      select(all_of(c(outcome, candidate))) %>%
      drop_na()
    model <- glm(
      reformulate(candidate, response = outcome),
      family = binomial(),
      data = model_data
    )
    tibble(
      term = candidate,
      n = nrow(model_data),
      p_value = wald_term_p(model, candidate),
      model = list(model)
    )
  }) %>%
    list_rbind()
}

title: Functions
text:
Backward elimination
backward_eliminate() starts with every candidate and repeatedly removes the variable with the largest P value, until all remaining variables have P below 0.05. The people analysed stay the same throughout: everyone with every candidate known, as Stata does. A variable that cannot be estimated in that group (it does not vary, or is fully determined by others) has no P value and is removed first, as Stata omits it.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Backward elimination for a logistic model (plan §8): start from every
# candidate on the complete cases for all of them (the sample stays fixed, as
# in Stata's stepwise), and repeatedly remove the term with the largest Wald
# P value while it is at or above `threshold`. A term with no estimable
# coefficient in that sample (no variation, P value NA) is removed first, as
# Stata omits it. Returns the final model, the fixed sample and the removal
# steps.
backward_eliminate <- function(data, outcome, candidates, threshold) {
  model_data <- data %>%
    select(all_of(c(outcome, candidates))) %>%
    drop_na()
  remaining <- candidates
  steps <- tibble(step = integer(), removed = character(), p_value = numeric())

  repeat {
    model <- glm(reformulate(remaining, response = outcome), family = binomial(), data = model_data)
    p_values <- map_dbl(remaining, \(term) wald_term_p(model, term))
    worst <- if (anyNA(p_values)) which(is.na(p_values))[1] else which.max(p_values)
    if (!is.na(p_values[worst]) && p_values[worst] < threshold) {
      break
    }
    steps <- add_row(steps, step = nrow(steps) + 1L, removed = remaining[worst], p_value = p_values[worst])
    remaining <- remaining[-worst]
    if (length(remaining) == 0) {
      model <- glm(reformulate("1", response = outcome), family = binomial(), data = model_data)
      break
    }
  }

  list(model = model, data = model_data, steps = steps, retained = remaining)
}

title: Functions
text:
Goodness of fit
hosmer_lemeshow() splits people into tenths by predicted risk and compares observed with expected deaths in each tenth.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Hosmer-Lemeshow goodness-of-fit test with `groups` groups of predicted risk
# (deciles by default): the statistic compares observed and expected events
# in each group, on groups - 2 degrees of freedom.
hosmer_lemeshow <- function(observed, predicted, groups = 10) {
  breaks <- unique(quantile(predicted, probs = seq(0, 1, length.out = groups + 1)))
  risk_group <- cut(predicted, breaks = breaks, include.lowest = TRUE)
  table <- tibble(observed, predicted, risk_group) %>%
    group_by(risk_group) %>%
    summarise(n = n(), observed = sum(observed), expected = sum(predicted), .groups = "drop")
  statistic <- sum((table$observed - table$expected)^2 / (table$expected * (1 - table$expected / table$n)))
  df <- nrow(table) - 2
  list(
    statistic = statistic,
    df = df,
    p_value = pchisq(statistic, df = df, lower.tail = FALSE),
    table = table
  )
}

title: Functions
text:
Small-count rules for tables
USRDS does not allow any count from 1 to 10 to be published, including one that can be worked out by subtraction. count_table_cells() lists every count behind a descriptive table, including the ones not printed (such as the number without a condition). flag_small_cells() marks the small ones and then, wherever a single hidden count could be recovered from a total, hides the next smallest count as well, repeating until nothing more changes. suppress_table_body() then puts “≤10” in those cells and removes the P value for that variable.


Click to show/hide R Code
# The counts behind a descriptive table, one row per variable, level and
# group: every level of a categorical variable, both TRUE and FALSE for a
# logical variable (only TRUE is shown in the table; FALSE can be derived),
# and the missing count. `groups` is the grouping column; an "Overall" group
# is added. Continuous variables contribute only their missing count.
count_table_cells <- function(data, variables, group) {
  long_data <- bind_rows(
    data %>% mutate(.group = as.character(.data[[group]])),
    data %>% mutate(.group = "Overall")
  )

  map(variables, \(variable) {
    values <- long_data[[variable]]
    level <- case_when(
      is.na(values) ~ "(missing)",
      is.numeric(values) ~ "(value)",
      .default = as.character(values)
    )
    tibble(variable = variable, level = level, group = long_data$.group) %>%
      count(variable, level, group) %>%
      complete(variable, level, group, fill = list(n = 0L)) %>%
      mutate(
        shown = case_when(
          level == "(value)" ~ FALSE,
          is.logical(values) & level == "FALSE" ~ FALSE,
          .default = TRUE
        )
      )
  }) %>%
    list_rbind()
}




Click to show/hide R Code
# Small-cell suppression (plan §10; USRDS rule: no count from 1 to
# `threshold`, including counts recoverable by subtraction). Input: one row
# per variable, level and group, with n and whether the cell is shown
# (FALSE for cells that are only derivable, such as the FALSE count of a
# logical variable, or continuous values). Returns the input with
# `suppress`: TRUE for every shown cell that must be hidden.
#   1. Primary: any cell (shown or derivable) with 1 to `threshold`.
#   2. Within a variable and group, the levels sum to the group size, so if
#      exactly one cell is unknown it can be recovered: hide the smallest
#      other non-zero shown cell.
#   3. Across groups, the groups sum to "Overall", so if exactly one cell of
#      a variable and level is unknown, hide the smallest other non-zero
#      shown cell.
# Rules 2 and 3 repeat until nothing changes. A derivable small cell counts
# as unknown only once another cell in its sum is hidden, which these rules
# ensure.
flag_small_cells <- function(counts, threshold = 10) {
  cells <- counts %>%
    mutate(unknown = n >= 1 & n <= threshold, .row = row_number())

  hide_one_more <- function(cells, by) {
    cells %>%
      group_by(across(all_of(by))) %>%
      mutate(
        .needs = sum(unknown) == 1,
        .candidate = shown & !unknown & n > 0,
        .pick = .needs & .candidate &
          n == suppressWarnings(min(n[.candidate])) &
          .row == suppressWarnings(min(.row[.candidate & n == min(n[.candidate])]))
      ) %>%
      ungroup() %>%
      mutate(unknown = unknown | .pick) %>%
      select(-.needs, -.candidate, -.pick)
  }

  repeat {
    before <- sum(cells$unknown)
    cells <- cells %>%
      hide_one_more(c("variable", "group")) %>%
      hide_one_more(c("variable", "level"))
    if (sum(cells$unknown) == before) {
      break
    }
  }

  unresolved <- cells %>%
    filter(unknown) %>%
    group_by(variable) %>%
    filter(!any(shown & unknown))
  if (nrow(unresolved) > 0) {
    warning(
      "Small derivable cells with no shown cell to hide in: ",
      str_flatten_comma(unique(unresolved$variable)),
      call. = FALSE
    )
  }

  cells %>%
    mutate(suppress = shown & unknown) %>%
    select(-unknown, -.row)
}




Click to show/hide R Code
# Apply small-cell flags (flag_small_cells()) to a gtsummary table body: the
# cells to hide are replaced with `mask`, and the P value of any variable
# with a hidden cell is removed (with the margins, a test statistic can
# reveal the hidden counts). `group_columns` maps group names in the flags to
# table columns (for example, c(Overall = "stat_0", ...)). Logical variables
# appear on their "label" row, other levels on "level" rows, and missing
# counts on the "missing" row.
suppress_table_body <- function(table_body, flags, group_columns, mask = "≤10") {
  hidden <- flags %>%
    filter(suppress) %>%
    mutate(
      row_type = case_when(
        level == "(missing)" ~ "missing",
        level == "TRUE" ~ "label",
        .default = "level"
      ),
      column = unname(group_columns[group])
    )

  for (i in seq_len(nrow(hidden))) {
    cell <- hidden[i, ]
    rows <- table_body$variable == cell$variable & table_body$row_type == cell$row_type
    if (cell$row_type == "level") {
      rows <- rows & table_body$label == cell$level
    }
    table_body[[cell$column]][rows] <- mask
  }

  if ("p.value" %in% names(table_body)) {
    table_body$p.value[table_body$variable %in% hidden$variable] <- NA
  }
  table_body
}

title: Functions
text:
Small-count rules for figures
km_reportable_times() picks the times the survival figure can show: more than 10 people still at risk, and every count and every change between times shown either 0 or above 10. flowchart_small_counts() lists any flowchart box with 1 to 10 people.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Times at which a Kaplan-Meier curve and risk table can be shown under the
# small-cell rule: more than `threshold` people still at risk (so the curve
# stops before its tail reveals small numbers), cumulative events and
# cumulative censored each 0 or above `threshold`, and every change since the
# previous time shown 0 or above `threshold`. Candidate times are tried in
# order; a time that fails is dropped and the next is compared with the last
# time kept. The curve should be drawn only up to the last time returned.
km_reportable_times <- function(km_fit, candidate_times, threshold = 10) {
  fit_summary <- summary(km_fit, times = candidate_times, extend = TRUE)
  table <- tibble(
    time = fit_summary$time,
    n_risk = fit_summary$n.risk,
    cum_event = cumsum(fit_summary$n.event),
    cum_censor = cumsum(fit_summary$n.censor)
  )
  allowed <- function(x) x == 0 | x > threshold

  kept <- integer()
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(table))) {
    current <- table[i, ]
    ok <- current$n_risk > threshold & allowed(current$cum_event) & allowed(current$cum_censor)
    if (length(kept) > 0) {
      previous <- table[last(kept), ]
      ok <- ok &
        allowed(previous$n_risk - current$n_risk) &
        allowed(current$cum_event - previous$cum_event) &
        allowed(current$cum_censor - previous$cum_censor)
    }
    if (ok) {
      kept <- c(kept, i)
    }
  }
  table$time[kept]
}




Click to show/hide R Code
# Boxes of a flowchart (the tibble from flowchart::fc_view(x, "fc"), with
# columns id, type, label and n) whose count is from 1 to `threshold`. Every
# exclusion is drawn with its own count (show_exc = TRUE), so no count is
# left to be recovered by subtraction; exported diagrams must return no rows.
flowchart_small_counts <- function(fc_boxes, threshold = 10) {
  fc_boxes %>%
    filter(!is.na(n), n >= 1, n <= threshold) %>%
    select(id, type, label, n)
}

title: Functions
text:
Odds ratios
tidy_odds_ratios() turns a fitted logistic model into odds ratios with 95% Wald confidence intervals (as Stata reports them) and readable labels.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Adjusted odds ratios with 95% Wald confidence intervals (as Stata's
# logistic reports them) from a logistic glm, one row per coefficient, with readable term labels from `labels` (a
# named character vector: variable name -> label) and the level appended for
# factors.
tidy_odds_ratios <- function(model, labels) {
  broom::tidy(model) %>%
    filter(term != "(Intercept)") %>%
    mutate(
      conf.low = exp(estimate - qnorm(0.975) * std.error),
      conf.high = exp(estimate + qnorm(0.975) * std.error),
      estimate = exp(estimate)
    ) %>%
    mutate(
      variable = map_chr(term, \(x) {
        matches <- names(labels)[str_starts(x, fixed(names(labels)))]
        if (length(matches) == 0) x else matches[which.max(nchar(matches))]
      }),
      level = str_remove(term, fixed(variable)),
      level = if_else(level %in% c("", "TRUE"), NA, level),
      term_label = if_else(
        is.na(level),
        unname(labels[variable]),
        str_c(unname(labels[variable]), ": ", level)
      )
    ) %>%
    select(term, term_label, estimate, conf.low, conf.high, p.value)
}
