Figure 1: the cohort
The flowchart is drawn from the same object that built the cohort, so the two cannot disagree. If any box holds 1 to 10 people, the figure is not saved and the run warns.


Click to show/hide R Code
# The flowchart from the same object that built the cohort, so the diagram
# and the analytic data cannot disagree. A box with 1 to 10 people is not
# exported: the run warns and the check is left for review.
flowchart_boxes <- flowchart::fc_view(cohort_flowchart, what = "fc")
flowchart_small <- flowchart_small_counts(flowchart_boxes)

if (nrow(flowchart_small) == 0) {
  cohort_flowchart %>%
    flowchart::fc_draw(big.mark = ",", box_corners = "sharp") %>%
    flowchart::fc_export("figure_1.png", path = "figures", width = 180, height = 240, units = "mm", res = 600) %>%
    flowchart::fc_export("figure_1.pdf", path = "figures", width = 180, height = 240, units = "mm")
} else {
  warning(
    "Figure 1 not exported: ", nrow(flowchart_small),
    " box(es) with 1 to 10 people (see flowchart_small).",
    call. = FALSE
  )
}


How this differs from the published figure. The published flowchart shows the starting totals and the final cohort only. This one shows every exclusion in the plan’s order, with its count, because a reader cannot judge who was left out otherwise (STROBE and RECORD item 13). Its boxes therefore will not line up one for one with the published ones.

title: Figures
text:
Figure 2: survival
The survival curve has its 95% confidence band and, below it, the number still at risk and the running totals of deaths and censored people. A time appears in that table only if no count shown there, or the change since the previous time, is from 1 to 10, and the curve stops at the last such time (km_reportable_times() on the Functions page). A dashed line marks 6 months.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Kaplan-Meier survival from the index admission (KMunicate style: curve with
# its 95% CI, and at risk, deaths and censored below). The risk table shows
# only times that pass the small-count rule, and the curve stops at the last
# of them (plan §10). Time 0 stays on the axis even when the table cannot
# show it (for example, 1 to 10 deaths on the admission day). A dashed line
# marks 6 months.
days_per_month <- 365.25 / 12
km_candidate_times <- c(0, mortality_window_days, seq(365, 10 * 365, by = 365))
km_times <- km_reportable_times(km_fit, km_candidate_times)
months_label <- \(days) round(days / days_per_month)

figure_2 <- ggsurvfit::ggsurvfit(
  km_fit,
  theme = theme_publication(),
  color = series_color,
  linewidth = 0.5
) +
  ggsurvfit::add_confidence_interval(fill = series_color, alpha = 0.15) +
  ggplot2::geom_vline(
    xintercept = mortality_window_days,
    linetype = "22", color = "gray40", linewidth = 0.3
  ) +
  ggsurvfit::add_risktable(
    times = km_times,
    risktable_stats = c("n.risk", "cum.censor", "cum.event"),
    stats_label = list(n.risk = "At risk", cum.censor = "Censored", cum.event = "Deaths"),
    theme = ggsurvfit::theme_risktable_default(axis.text.y.size = 8, plot.title.size = 8),
    size = 2.4
  ) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = union(0, km_times),
    labels = months_label,
    limits = c(0, max(km_times)),
    expand = ggplot2::expansion(add = c(60, 200))
  ) +
  ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(
    labels = scales::label_percent(),
    limits = c(0, 1),
    expand = ggplot2::expansion(mult = c(0, 0.02))
  ) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "Months since index admission", y = "Probability of survival")

save_figure(figure_2, file.path("figures", "figure_2"), width = 170, height = 120)


How this differs from the published figure. The published curve shows years on the axis, the number at risk every 5 years, and no confidence band. This one follows the KMunicate recommendations: the 95% confidence band, and below the curve the numbers at risk, censored and dead at each time shown, so a reader can see how much information lies behind each part of the curve. Time is in months, because the outcome is at 6 months.

title: Figures
text:
Figure 3: odds ratios
Each variable kept in the final model, with its adjusted odds ratio and 95% confidence interval on a log scale, and the numbers printed beside it.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Adjusted odds ratios from the final model, with 95% Wald CIs, on a log
# scale (halving and doubling the odds are equal distances), with ticks at
# 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4 and 8 so the scale is plain; the estimate and interval
# are printed beside each row, written "a to b" as in the tables (AMA style).
odds_ratios <- tidy_odds_ratios(multivariable$model, report_labels) %>%
  mutate(
    term_label = fct_rev(fct_inorder(term_label)),
    or_text = str_glue(
      "{scales::number(estimate, accuracy = 0.01)} ",
      "({scales::number(conf.low, accuracy = 0.01)} to {scales::number(conf.high, accuracy = 0.01)})"
    )
  )
or_text_x <- max(odds_ratios$conf.high) * 1.6

figure_3 <- ggplot2::ggplot(odds_ratios, ggplot2::aes(x = estimate, y = term_label)) +
  ggplot2::geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "22", color = "gray40", linewidth = 0.3) +
  ggplot2::geom_pointrange(
    ggplot2::aes(xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high),
    color = series_color, size = 0.3, linewidth = 0.4
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_text(
    ggplot2::aes(x = or_text_x, label = or_text),
    hjust = 0, size = 2.6, color = "gray20"
  ) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_log10(
    breaks = c(0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8),
    labels = scales::label_number(drop0trailing = TRUE),
    expand = ggplot2::expansion(mult = c(0.05, 0.45))
  ) +
  ggplot2::coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "Adjusted odds ratio (95% CI), log scale", y = NULL) +
  ggplot2::theme(panel.grid.major.y = ggplot2::element_blank())

save_figure(
  figure_3, file.path("figures", "figure_3"),
  width = 160, height = 30 + 8 * nrow(odds_ratios)
)


How this differs from the published figure. The published forest plot uses a linear axis from 0 to 10. This one uses a log scale, on which halving and doubling the odds are the same distance from 1, so effects in either direction can be compared by eye; the estimate and interval are printed beside each row so no value has to be read off the axis.

Captions and alt text
Captions and descriptions for screen readers are built from the fitted results, so no number is typed by hand.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Captions and alt text, built from the fitted objects so no number is
# retyped.
list_or_none <- \(x) if (length(x) == 0) "none" else str_flatten_comma(as.character(x), ", and ")
six_month_survival <- summary(km_fit, times = mortality_window_days)$surv
reference_levels <- multivariable$model$xlevels %>%
  imap_chr(\(levels, variable) str_c(report_labels[[variable]], ": ", dplyr::first(levels)))
figure_text <- tibble(
  figure = c("figure_1", "figure_2", "figure_3"),
  caption = c(
    "Figure 1. Selection of kidney transplant recipients hospitalized with cryptococcosis, USRDS 2006-2016.",
    str_glue(
      "Figure 2. Kaplan-Meier estimate of overall survival from the index admission, with 95% confidence interval. ",
      "The dashed line marks 6 months. Numbers below are people at risk and cumulative censored and deaths; ",
      "the curve stops at the last time with more than 10 people at risk (USRDS data use agreement)."
    ),
    str_c(
      "Figure 3. Adjusted odds ratios for death within 6 months of admission, from the final logistic model after backward elimination, with 95% confidence intervals (log scale).",
      if (length(reference_levels) > 0) str_c(" Reference categories: ", str_flatten(reference_levels, "; "), ".") else ""
    )
  ),
  alt_text = c(
    str_glue(
      "Flowchart of {nrow(flowchart_boxes %>% filter(type == 'exclude'))} exclusion steps, from people with a cryptococcosis ",
      "hospitalization to the {scales::label_comma()(nrow(cohort))} recipients in the analysis."
    ),
    str_glue(
      "Single Kaplan-Meier survival curve over {months_label(max(km_times))} months after admission; ",
      "survival at 6 months is {scales::label_percent(accuracy = 0.1)(six_month_survival)}."
    ),
    str_glue(
      "Forest plot of {nrow(odds_ratios)} adjusted odds ratios. ",
      "Confidence intervals entirely above 1: ",
      "{list_or_none(odds_ratios$term_label[odds_ratios$conf.low > 1])}; ",
      "entirely below 1: ",
      "{list_or_none(odds_ratios$term_label[odds_ratios$conf.high < 1])}."
    )
  )
)
write_csv(figure_text, file.path("figures", "figure_text.csv"))

title: Published supplement
text:
Notes on the supplement
These are kept above as printed and listed so this analysis’s code lists can be compared with them. How each was handled is on the Code lists page and in the linked issues.

Cryptococcosis lists the ICD-10-CM category B45 itself as well as its subcodes. ICD-10-CM has no codes B45.4 to B45.6, so the subcodes listed are all of them.
Diabetes marks 250, E08, E09, E10, E11 and E13 with an asterisk, meaning every code beginning with them; the other codes are matched exactly (#8).
Procedures are ICD procedure codes only. The paper’s Methods mention CPT codes, which the supplement does not list (#5). There is no separate row for the ventriculoperitoneal shunts the paper reports; the shunt codes are among the neurosurgical procedures (#8).
Medications are listed as HCPCS billing codes for cyclosporine and tacrolimus. The paper describes its drug data both ways: its Methods say drug information at UNOS registration and the first post-transplant visit “was obtained using relevant billing codes”, while the title of its Table 2 names the UNOS registration and follow-up appointment. This analysis uses the UNOS records (#2).
Some ICD-9 procedure codes have only three digits (031, 034, 321, 326 and 329). These are complete codes with no subcodes, and are matched exactly. 022 was also a complete code until October 2012, when it was split into 02.21 and 02.22, both of which are listed too.

title: Overview
text: Cryptococcosis is an invasive fungal infection that affects people with weakened immune systems, including kidney transplant recipients. Fiorica et al. used USRDS data to study 6-month mortality, and the factors associated with it, among kidney transplant recipients hospitalized with cryptococcosis from 2006 to 20161. The Background pages say more about the disease, the data and the statistical methods.

title: Overview
text:
What this project does
This project replicates that analysis as the paper describes it, using the usRds R package wherever the package can do a step. Along the way it assesses how well usRds covers the paper’s methods.
The original analysis was run in Stata, and that code is no longer available. The paper and its supplement are therefore the specification. The published estimates are a reference point, not a target.

title: Overview
Overview
text:
Status
In progress; nothing on this site comes from USRDS data. The code covers every step from the cohort to the tables and figures, and runs end to end on synthetic data; it has not yet been run on the USRDS data. The paper’s own results are on the Published results pages, and the differences from the reconstruction of the original analysis are listed. Open decisions are tracked as decision issues.

title: Tables
text: This script makes Tables 1 and 2 (characteristics and immunosuppression by vital status 6 months after admission) and the odds-ratio table, following plan §8 and the disclosure rules in §10. The tables are written to tables/, which is not in the repository; they appear on this site only after USRDS review clears them.

title: Tables
text:
Journal style
The tables follow the style shared by OFID, CID and JID, which is AMA style: gtsummary’s JAMA theme, with P values shown without a leading zero (style_pvalue_ama() on the Functions page).


Click to show/hide R Code
# OFID, CID and JID share one house style, which follows the AMA Manual of
# Style (OFID author guidelines; plan §8). gtsummary's JAMA theme gives the
# AMA conventions: P values to 2 decimals without a leading zero, "No. (%)"
# and the statistic named beside each variable, and CIs written "a to b".
# On top of it, P values drop the leading zero (style_pvalue_ama()), and
# footnotes use lowercase letters when the tables are saved.
gtsummary::theme_gtsummary_journal("jama")
gtsummary::set_gtsummary_theme(list(
  "pkgwide-fn:pvalue_fun" = style_pvalue_ama,
  "pkgwide-fn:prependpvalue_fun" = \(x) str_c("P", if_else(str_detect(style_pvalue_ama(x), "^[<>]"), " ", " = "), style_pvalue_ama(x))
))
p_value_header <- "***P*** **value**"

title: Tables
text:
Descriptive tables
One function makes both descriptive tables. Continuous variables are shown as mean (SD), time since transplant as median (IQR), and everything else as a count and percentage, with the number unknown always shown. Continuous variables are compared with Student’s t test; categorical ones with the chi-squared test, or Fisher’s exact test when an expected count is under 5.
Before the table is shown, every count from 1 to 10 is hidden, along with any other count that would let it be worked out by subtraction, and the P value of that variable is removed (flag_small_cells() and suppress_table_body() on the Functions page).


Click to show/hide R Code
# One descriptive table by vital status (plan §8): mean (SD) for continuous
# variables, median (IQR) for time since transplant, No. (%) otherwise, with
# missing counts always shown. Student t test for continuous variables; for
# categorical ones, the chi-squared test without continuity correction, or
# Fisher's exact test when an expected count is under 5 (gtsummary's
# default rule). Small cells are then hidden (plan §10).
describe_by_vital_status <- function(data, variables, labels, medians = character()) {
  counts <- count_table_cells(data, variables, group = "vital_status")
  flags <- flag_small_cells(counts)

  table <- data %>%
    select(all_of(c("vital_status", variables))) %>%
    gtsummary::tbl_summary(
      by = vital_status,
      label = as.list(labels[variables]),
      statistic = c(
        list(gtsummary::all_continuous() ~ "{mean} ({sd})"),
        as.list(set_names(rep("{median} ({p25} \u2013 {p75})", length(medians)), medians))
      ),
      digits = list(gtsummary::all_categorical() ~ c(0, 1)),
      missing = "always",
      missing_text = "Unknown"
    ) %>%
    gtsummary::add_overall(last = FALSE) %>%
    gtsummary::add_p(
      test = list(gtsummary::all_continuous() ~ "t.test"),
      test.args = list(gtsummary::all_continuous() ~ list(var.equal = TRUE))
    ) %>%
    gtsummary::modify_table_body(
      \(body) suppress_table_body(body, flags, table_group_columns) %>%
        mutate(stat_label = str_replace(stat_label, "^n \\(%\\)$", "No. (%)"))
    ) %>%
    gtsummary::modify_header(p.value = p_value_header) %>%
    gtsummary::modify_footnote_header(
      "Cells with 1 to 10 people, and cells from which they could be recovered, are shown as ≤10, and their P values are removed (USRDS data use agreement).",
      columns = gtsummary::all_stat_cols(),
      replace = FALSE
    )

  list(table = table, flags = flags)
}

title: Tables
text:
Follow-up
Before any model, how long people were followed and how many died or were censored. Median follow-up uses the reverse Kaplan–Meier method, which treats censoring as the event.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Follow-up before any model (time to event): deaths, censoring, and median
# follow-up by the reverse Kaplan-Meier method (censoring treated as the
# event). Counts here pass the same small-count rule as the tables.
reverse_km <- survival::survfit(
  survival::Surv(survival_days, 1 - survival_event) ~ 1,
  data = analysis_data
)
follow_up_summary <- tibble(
  measure = c(
    "People", "Deaths", "Censored",
    "Deaths within 6 months", "Median follow-up, days (95% CI)"
  ),
  value = c(
    nrow(analysis_data),
    sum(analysis_data$survival_event),
    sum(analysis_data$survival_event == 0),
    sum(model_data$died_within_window),
    str_glue(
      "{summary(reverse_km)$table[['median']]} ",
      "({summary(reverse_km)$table[['0.95LCL']]}, {summary(reverse_km)$table[['0.95UCL']]})"
    )
  ) %>%
    as.character()
)

title: Tables
text:
Odds ratios
Each variable alone, and the final model after backward elimination, side by side. The P value shown for each variable is the single joint test the selection used, so a variable with several categories has one P value, not one per category.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Unadjusted (each candidate alone) and adjusted (final backward-elimination
# model) odds ratios with 95% Wald confidence intervals. P values are the
# joint Wald P per term that the selection used (plan §8), one per variable,
# not one per factor level. Candidates with no estimable coefficient (no
# variation among the people with them known) are listed in a footnote.
replace_term_p <- function(body, term_p) {
  body %>%
    left_join(term_p, by = "variable") %>%
    mutate(p.value = if_else(row_type == "label", term_p_value, NA_real_)) %>%
    select(-term_p_value)
}

estimable <- bivariable_results %>% filter(!is.na(p_value))
not_estimable <- bivariable_results %>% filter(is.na(p_value))
# Yes/no variables are shown on one row (the odds ratio for yes)
logical_terms <- estimable$term[map_lgl(model_data[estimable$term], is.logical)]

table_unadjusted <- model_data %>%
  select(all_of(c("died_within_window", estimable$term))) %>%
  gtsummary::tbl_uvregression(
    method = glm,
    y = died_within_window,
    method.args = list(family = binomial),
    exponentiate = TRUE,
    label = as.list(report_labels[estimable$term]),
    show_single_row = all_of(logical_terms),
    hide_n = TRUE
  ) %>%
  gtsummary::modify_table_body(
    \(body) replace_term_p(body, tibble(variable = estimable$term, term_p_value = estimable$p_value))
  )

adjusted_p <- tibble(
  variable = multivariable$retained,
  term_p_value = map_dbl(multivariable$retained, \(term) wald_term_p(multivariable$model, term))
)
table_adjusted <- multivariable$model %>%
  gtsummary::tbl_regression(
    exponentiate = TRUE,
    label = as.list(report_labels[multivariable$retained]),
    show_single_row = all_of(intersect(logical_terms, multivariable$retained))
  ) %>%
  gtsummary::modify_table_body(\(body) replace_term_p(body, adjusted_p))

model_n <- nobs(multivariable$model)
model_events <- sum(multivariable$data$died_within_window)
model_excluded <- nrow(model_data) - model_n

table_models <- gtsummary::tbl_merge(
  list(table_unadjusted, table_adjusted),
  tab_spanner = c("**Unadjusted**", "**Adjusted**")
) %>%
  gtsummary::modify_header(p.value_1 = p_value_header, p.value_2 = p_value_header) %>%
  gtsummary::modify_caption("**Table 3.** Odds ratios for death within 6 months of admission") %>%
  gtsummary::modify_source_note(
    str_glue(
      "Unadjusted: one logistic model per variable, on the people with it known. ",
      "Adjusted: backward elimination from all candidates (removed while P ≥ {elimination_threshold}), ",
      "on the {model_n} people with every candidate known ({model_events} deaths; {model_excluded} excluded for missing data). ",
      "P values are joint Wald tests, one per variable. ",
      "Hosmer-Lemeshow test of the adjusted model: χ² = {round(hosmer_lemeshow_result$statistic, 2)}, ",
      "df = {hosmer_lemeshow_result$df}, P = {gtsummary::style_pvalue(hosmer_lemeshow_result$p_value, digits = 2)}."
    )
  )
if (nrow(not_estimable) > 0) {
  table_models <- table_models %>%
    gtsummary::modify_source_note(
      str_c("Not estimable (no variation): ", str_flatten_comma(report_labels[not_estimable$term]), ".")
    )
}

format_or <- function(estimate, low, high, accuracy = 0.01) {
  str_glue(
    "{scales::number(estimate, accuracy = accuracy)} ",
    "({scales::number(low, accuracy = accuracy)} to {scales::number(high, accuracy = accuracy)})"
  )
}
published_comparison <- published_model %>%
  left_join(
    tidy_odds_ratios(published_fit, report_labels) %>%
      mutate(term = str_remove(term, "TRUE$")) %>%
      select(term, term_label, estimate, conf.low, conf.high),
    by = "term"
  ) %>%
  transmute(
    Characteristic = term_label,
    `Published aOR (95% CI)` = format_or(published_or, published_low, published_high, accuracy = 0.1),
    `This analysis, aOR (95% CI)` = format_or(estimate, conf.low, conf.high),
    `Kept by backward elimination` = if_else(term %in% multivariable$retained, "Yes", "No")
  )
table_published_model <- published_comparison %>%
  gt::gt() %>%
  gt::tab_caption(gt::md("**Table 4.** The paper's final model refitted, beside the published adjusted odds ratios")) %>%
  gt::tab_source_note(str_glue(
    "Published estimates: Fiorica et al. 2025, Results. This analysis: the same eight terms in one logistic model, ",
    "on the {nobs(published_fit)} people with every candidate known ({sum(multivariable$data$died_within_window)} deaths), as in Table 3. ",
    "Abbreviation: aOR = adjusted odds ratio."
  ))

title: Tables
text:
Disclosure checks
Some counts cannot be hidden inside a table, such as how many people the model left out for missing data. They are collected here for the reviewer; any row marked for review must be resolved before results leave the approved environment.


Click to show/hide R Code
# What a reviewer needs before release (plan §10): cells hidden in each
# table, and counts the tables cannot hide themselves. Rows with
# needs_review = TRUE must be resolved before anything leaves the approved
# environment.
group_sizes <- table(table_data$vital_status)
disclosure_checks <- tibble(
  check = c(
    "Table 1: cells hidden",
    "Table 2: cells hidden",
    "Smallest vital-status group",
    "People excluded from the adjusted model for missing data",
    "Deaths in the adjusted model",
    "Smallest of deaths and censored in follow-up"
  ),
  value = c(
    sum(table_1_result$flags$suppress),
    sum(table_2_result$flags$suppress),
    min(group_sizes),
    model_excluded,
    model_events,
    min(sum(analysis_data$survival_event), sum(analysis_data$survival_event == 0))
  ),
  needs_review = c(
    FALSE,
    FALSE,
    min(group_sizes) <= 10,
    between(model_excluded, 1, 10),
    between(model_events, 1, 10),
    between(min(sum(analysis_data$survival_event), sum(analysis_data$survival_event == 0)), 1, 10)
  )
)




Click to show/hide R Code
dir.create("tables", showWarnings = FALSE)
walk2(
  list(table_1, table_2, table_models),
  c("table_1", "table_2", "table_models"),
  \(table, name) {
    gt_table <- gtsummary::as_gt(table) %>%
      gt::opt_footnote_marks(marks = "letters")
    gt::gtsave(gt_table, file.path("tables", str_c(name, ".html")))
    gt::gtsave(gt_table, file.path("tables", str_c(name, ".docx")))
  }
)
gt::gtsave(table_published_model, file.path("tables", "table_published_model.html"))
gt::gtsave(table_published_model, file.path("tables", "table_published_model.docx"))

This script builds the characteristics the analysis compares and models, listed in §5 of the analysis plan. It joins them to the cohort to give analysis_data, with one row per person.

title: Covariates
text:
Starting point
Each person’s index stay, from the cohort.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Columns are chosen with select() after loading, not with col_select,
# because load_usrds_file() fails on Parquet files when col_select is used
# (usRds#22). Return to col_select once that is fixed.
# The cohort's index stays, the starting point for every covariate.
cohort_index <- cohort %>%
  select(USRDS_ID, index_admit_date, index_discharge_date)

cohort_ids <- cohort_index$USRDS_ID

title: Covariates
text:
Hospitalization records
All hospitalization records of cohort members are loaded from both files through usRds. Each record is flagged for the diagnoses and procedures of interest, using each file’s own code columns.


Click to show/hide R Code
# All hospitalization records of cohort members, with diagnosis and procedure
# columns and ICU/CCU days. usRds gap (coverage map, steps 4-9): searched here.
dx_concepts <- c(index_stay_dx_concepts, "transplant_complication")

hospitalization_records <- bind_rows(
  load_flagged_hospitalizations(
    "hosp_to2009", cohort_ids, hosp_to2009_dx_columns, hosp_to2009_proc_columns,
    dx_concepts, index_stay_proc_concepts, code_lists
  ),
  load_flagged_hospitalizations(
    "hosp_2010on", cohort_ids, hosp_2010on_dx_columns, hosp_2010on_proc_columns,
    dx_concepts, index_stay_proc_concepts, code_lists
  )
)

title: Covariates
text:
On the index stay
These are taken from the records that make up the index stay:

meningitis, acute kidney injury, diabetes and cirrhosis;
the five procedure groups;
ICU admission (any ICU or CCU days).



Click to show/hide R Code
# Meningitis, acute kidney injury, diabetes, cirrhosis and procedures on any
# record of the index stay; ICU admission if any ICU or CCU days.
index_stay_covariates <- summarise_index_stay(
  hospitalization_records,
  cohort_index,
  c(index_stay_dx_concepts, index_stay_proc_concepts)

Earlier hospitalization for a transplant complication
Whether any hospitalization before the index admission had a transplant-complication code.

title: Covariates
text:
Transplant history, sex and race
These come from the USRDS transplant file:

how many transplants, and graft failures, came before the index admission;
how long it had been since the most recent transplant;
sex and race, from that most recent transplant’s record.



Click to show/hide R Code
# Transplants, graft failures and time since the most recent transplant, from
# the USRDS transplant file. Sex and race come from the record of the most
# recent transplant, as in the reconstruction (which took them from this file).
transplants <- load_usrds_file(
  "tx",
  usrds_ids = cohort_ids,
  factor_labels = FALSE
) %>%
  select(all_of(c("USRDS_ID", "TDATE", "FAILDATE", "RSEX", "RACE")))

transplant_history <- summarise_transplant_history(transplants, cohort_index)

transplant_demographics <- transplants %>%
  inner_join(
    transplant_history %>% select(USRDS_ID, last_transplant_date),
    by = c("USRDS_ID", "TDATE" = "last_transplant_date"),
    relationship = "many-to-one"
  ) %>%
  distinct(USRDS_ID, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  transmute(USRDS_ID, sex = recode_sex(RSEX), race = recode_race(RACE))

title: Covariates
text:
Ethnicity and region
These come from the patients file. Hispanic ethnicity follows the official coding, and region uses the region table.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Hispanic ethnicity and region of residence, from the patients file.
patient_covariates <- load_usrds_file(
  "patients",
  usrds_ids = cohort_ids,
  factor_labels = FALSE
) %>%
  select(all_of(c("USRDS_ID", "HISPANIC", "STATE"))) %>%

title: Covariates
text:
Registry data at transplant
BMI, dialysis before transplant, HIV and CMV status, and rejection come from the UNOS registration of the most recent transplant on or before the index admission. Kidney-alone and kidney–pancreas registrations are stacked together.


Click to show/hide R Code
# UNOS registration of the most recent transplant on or before the index
# admission (kidney-alone and kidney-pancreas files stacked; the kidney-
# pancreas file names kidney rejection ACUTE_REJ_EPI_KI).
registration_columns <- c(
  "USRDS_ID", unos_registration_id, "TDATE", "BMI", "PRE_TX_DIAL",
  "HIV_SEROSTATUS", "CMV_STATUS"
)

registrations <- bind_rows(
  load_usrds_file(
    "txunos_trr_ki",
    usrds_ids = cohort_ids,
    factor_labels = FALSE
  ) %>%
    select(all_of(c(registration_columns, "ACUTE_REJ_EPI"))) %>%
    mutate(organ = "Kidney"),
  load_usrds_file(
    "txunos_trr_kp",
    usrds_ids = cohort_ids,
    factor_labels = FALSE
  ) %>%
    select(all_of(c(registration_columns, "ACUTE_REJ_EPI_KI"))) %>%
    rename(ACUTE_REJ_EPI = ACUTE_REJ_EPI_KI) %>%
    mutate(organ = "Kidney-pancreas")
)

index_registration <- select_index_registration(registrations, cohort_index)

title: Covariates
text:
Registry follow-up reports
The follow-up reports of that same transplant. A report without a date takes the date the kidney graft failed, as in the reconstruction.

Decision pending: the name of the key linking follow-up drug records to these reports has to be confirmed for the release in use (see Setup).



Click to show/hide R Code
# Follow-up reports of the index registration. A missing FUDATE falls back to
# the kidney graft failure date (FUKIFAIL), as in the reconstruction.
followup_columns <- c(
  "USRDS_ID", unos_registration_id, unos_followup_id, "FUDATE", "FUKIFAIL"
)

followups <- bind_rows(
  load_usrds_file(
    "txfuunos_ki",
    usrds_ids = cohort_ids,
    factor_labels = FALSE
  ) %>%
    select(all_of(c(followup_columns, "ACUTE_REJ_EPI"))),
  load_usrds_file(
    "txfuunos_kp",
    usrds_ids = cohort_ids,
    factor_labels = FALSE
  ) %>%
    select(all_of(c(followup_columns, "ACUTE_REJ_EPI_KI"))) %>%
    rename(ACUTE_REJ_EPI = ACUTE_REJ_EPI_KI)
) %>%
  mutate(FUDATE = coalesce(FUDATE, FUKIFAIL)) %>%
  semi_join(index_registration, by = c("USRDS_ID", unos_registration_id)) %>%
  inner_join(cohort_index %>% select(USRDS_ID, index_admit_date), by = "USRDS_ID", relationship = "many-to-one")

title: Covariates
text:
Acute rejection
A person counts as having had acute rejection if there was any episode, treated or not:

at the registration, or
on a follow-up report dated before the index admission.

The same section also puts the other registration values into analysis form: BMI as recorded, dialysis as yes or no, and HIV and CMV status as positive or negative. Unknown codes are missing. An alternative is to use claims coded for kidney transplant rejection; that is described in the plan but not built (§9).


Click to show/hide R Code
# Acute rejection: any episode (ACREJEPI 1 or 2) at the index registration or
# on a follow-up report of that transplant dated before the index admission
# (decided 2026-11-10). An ICD claims definition (T86.11) is the alternative
# (plan §9); it is not built here.
followup_rejection <- followups %>%
  filter(FUDATE < index_admit_date) %>%
  group_by(USRDS_ID) %>%
  summarise(rejection_followup = any_known(unos_rejection_any(ACUTE_REJ_EPI)), .groups = "drop")

registration_covariates <- index_registration %>%
  left_join(followup_rejection, by = "USRDS_ID", relationship = "one-to-one") %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(
    acute_rejection = any_known(c(unos_rejection_any(ACUTE_REJ_EPI), rejection_followup))
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  transmute(
    USRDS_ID,
    organ,
    bmi = BMI,
    pretransplant_dialysis = case_when(
      PRE_TX_DIAL == "Y" ~ TRUE,
      PRE_TX_DIAL == "N" ~ FALSE,
      .default = NA
    ),
    hiv_status = case_when(HIV_SEROSTATUS == "P" ~ "Positive", HIV_SEROSTATUS == "N" ~ "Negative", .default = NA),
    cmv_status = case_when(CMV_STATUS == "P" ~ "Positive", CMV_STATUS == "N" ~ "Negative", .default = NA),
    acute_rejection
  )

title: Covariates
text:
Immunosuppression at transplant
The drug classes recorded at that transplant’s registration (#2). A registration with no drug records is missing rather than “not on”.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Immunosuppression at transplant: the index registration's drug records
# (TXIRUNOS), any drug in each class. A registration with no drug records is
# missing, not "not on".
transplant_drugs <- load_usrds_file(
  "txirunos",
  usrds_ids = cohort_ids,
  factor_labels = FALSE
) %>%
  select(all_of(c("USRDS_ID", unos_registration_id, "RX_CD", "DRUG_CD_OSTXT"))) %>%
  semi_join(index_registration, by = c("USRDS_ID", unos_registration_id))

immunosuppression_transplant <- classify_immunosuppressants(
  transplant_drugs,
  unos_registration_id,
  immunosuppressant_classes,
  immunosuppressant_free_text
) %>%
  inner_join(
    index_registration %>% select(USRDS_ID, all_of(unos_registration_id)),
    by = unos_registration_id,
    relationship = "one-to-one"
  ) %>%
  select(-all_of(unos_registration_id)) %>%
  rename_with(\(x) str_c("tx_", x), -USRDS_ID)

title: Covariates
text:
Immunosuppression at first follow-up
The drug classes current at that transplant’s first follow-up visit, as the paper’s Methods describe (#2). A drug counts only if it was current maintenance at the visit.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Immunosuppression at the first follow-up report of the index transplant
# (earliest FUDATE, whatever its date relative to the index admission; #2):
# a class counts if one of its drugs is current maintenance (RXMNTCUR = 1).
first_followup <- followups %>%
  filter(!is.na(FUDATE)) %>%
  group_by(USRDS_ID) %>%
  slice_min(FUDATE, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(USRDS_ID, all_of(unos_followup_id))

followup_drugs <- load_usrds_file(
  "txifunos",
  usrds_ids = cohort_ids,
  factor_labels = FALSE
) %>%
  select(all_of(c("USRDS_ID", unos_followup_id, "RX_CD", "DRUG_CD_OSTXT", "RXMNTCUR"))) %>%
  semi_join(first_followup, by = c("USRDS_ID", unos_followup_id)) %>%
  # Drugs not current at the visit keep the follow-up's key but match no class
  mutate(
    RX_CD = if_else(RXMNTCUR %in% 1, RX_CD, NA),
    DRUG_CD_OSTXT = if_else(RXMNTCUR %in% 1, DRUG_CD_OSTXT, NA)
  )

immunosuppression_followup <- classify_immunosuppressants(
  followup_drugs,
  unos_followup_id,
  immunosuppressant_classes,
  immunosuppressant_free_text
) %>%
  inner_join(first_followup, by = unos_followup_id, relationship = "one-to-one") %>%
  select(-all_of(unos_followup_id)) %>%
  rename_with(\(x) str_c("fu_", x), -USRDS_ID)

title: Covariates
text:
Putting it together
Every covariate table is joined to the cohort one-to-one, so a duplicate stops the run. Time since transplant is converted to months and also split at the plan’s 2-year cut-off. The script then checks that analysis_data still has exactly one row per cohort member.


Click to show/hide R Code
# One row per cohort member. Joins are one-to-one, so a duplicate stops the run.
analysis_data <- cohort %>%
  left_join(index_stay_covariates, by = "USRDS_ID", relationship = "one-to-one") %>%
  left_join(prior_complication, by = "USRDS_ID", relationship = "one-to-one") %>%
  left_join(transplant_history, by = "USRDS_ID", relationship = "one-to-one") %>%
  left_join(transplant_demographics, by = "USRDS_ID", relationship = "one-to-one") %>%
  left_join(patient_covariates, by = "USRDS_ID", relationship = "one-to-one") %>%
  left_join(registration_covariates, by = "USRDS_ID", relationship = "one-to-one") %>%
  left_join(immunosuppression_transplant, by = "USRDS_ID", relationship = "one-to-one") %>%
  left_join(immunosuppression_followup, by = "USRDS_ID", relationship = "one-to-one") %>%
  mutate(
    months_since_last_transplant = days_since_last_transplant / (365.25 / 12),
    over_cutoff_since_transplant = days_since_last_transplant > years_since_transplant_cutoff * 365.25
  )

stopifnot(nrow(analysis_data) == nrow(cohort))

Project documentsAGENTS.md Code

The project
This is an R analysis project, not an R package. It rebuilds the analysis of Fiorica et al. 2025 (6-month mortality, and the factors associated with it, among kidney transplant recipients hospitalized with cryptococcosis, USRDS 2006–2016) with the usRds package. The goal is to replicate the analysis as the paper describes it, and in doing so to assess how well usRds covers it. For each step, references/usrds-coverage.md records whether usRds does it (covered, partial or gap). Closing gaps in usRds is outside this project’s scope; findings are passed to the usRds maintainer, who decides what to do with them. The code and methods are published as a Quarto website.

What counts as done for a step. A step is done when it runs on synthetic data, using usRds functions where they exist and project code in R/functions.R where they don’t, and its coverage status in references/usrds-coverage.md reflects what the code actually needed. Project code written for a gap is labelled as such in a comment, so the assessment can be read from the code. The published counts and odds ratios are a reference point, not a target: the original analysis was run in Stata, that code is no longer available, and the data release may differ. A difference from the paper is investigated, but it is not a defect unless it comes from departing from the paper’s methods or from a usRds error.
The paper is the specification; the legacy Rmd is secondary evidence. The 2025-03-25 Rmd is the maintainer’s best reconstruction of how the original Stata analysis was done; it did not produce the published results. Where the paper (including its supplement) states a method, the plan follows the paper. Where the paper is silent, the Rmd’s choice is a candidate for the deciders, not a default; where the two disagree, the paper wins and the difference is noted, unless a decision says otherwise (the code lists come from the Rmd by decision, with corrections checked against the official code sets; see the plan, §5) (see #4). Do not introduce package infrastructure or impose CRAN conventions.
The analysis plan is the scientific source of truth. Code implements the plan; it does not redefine it. If implementation needs a different design, open a decision issue, or comment on the existing one, for the deciders. Once a decider has settled it (in the issue, or relayed there in their exact words), the plan change and the code can go in the same pull request, which closes the issue. Track decisions in Git history and issues rather than a change ledger within the plan.
Deciders. Scientific decisions in every area are made by Vagish Hemmige. Anyone may open or contribute to a decision issue; only a decider settles it (see “Working with agents”).
Do not make unresolved scientific decisions implicitly through code. Check relevant open GitHub issues before implementing analyses that depend on them.
Maintain implementation status and defects in GitHub Issues rather than in a standing list inside this file.
Default branch: main. Changes reach it only through pull requests.

Data sources
Each source this project uses is listed below with the package that accesses it. Code that touches a source goes through its package. Do not write project-specific loading, cleaning, or definition code for something the package already does.











Source
Accessed through
Package documentation
Package maintained by
Access
What AI agents may do

usRds (load_usrds_file(), get_IN_ICD(), get_PS_ICD())
https://vagishhemmige.github.io/usRds/
This team
Restricted (USRDS data use agreement)

To allow more for a source, a person changes its row through a pull request, naming the agreement and section that permit it, the approved AI service, and exactly what agents may do. Agents never propose or make this change themselves, and nothing in personal instructions can grant it.
Add a row when code first loads a new source. The UNOS transplant files (txunos_trr_ki, txunos_trr_kp, txfuunos_*, txirunos) are part of the USRDS release and are covered by the row above.
For every package:

Read its documentation before writing code for a source, including known issues. Behavior that sets the cohort, an exposure, an outcome, or a denominator is checked in the documentation, not assumed from a function’s name.

For packages this team maintains: see “Look in usRds first” below.
For external packages:

Work around problems here. Wrap the function in R/functions.R with a comment explaining the problem and linking any upstream issue. Reporting a bug upstream is an external communication; the person directing the work decides whether to file it.
Facts about the source that this project relies on (definitions, release quirks, suppression rules) go in references/ with a citation to the provider’s documentation, or in the plan when they shape a decision.

For a source with no package: one loading script records the download URL, the release or access date, and any processing. Verify its variables against the provider’s documentation for that release.

Exploration and definitive analysis
Exploration is welcome on branches or forks. Experimental scripts need not be sourced from R/main.R or have Quarto pages, and their findings are labelled preliminary. A script becomes part of the definitive analysis when it is sourced from R/main.R; from then on every rule below applies to it.

R scripts

Open the .Rproj and run R/main.R from the project root. main.R sources definitive scripts in dependency order.
Keep scripts focused on one analytical responsibility. Study-specific scripts may be grouped in stage-specific subdirectories. Include a short header stating the script’s role, its required upstream objects, and what it produces.
When a definitive script is added or structurally reorganized, source it in main.R as appropriate and update ARCHITECTURE.md in the same pull request when the change materially affects structure or data flow. ARCHITECTURE.md describes current implementation, not planned work.
Define shared libraries, paths, configurable analytical constants, and their dependencies in R/setup.R. Other scripts do not call library(), re-source setup.R, or hard-code study parameters. Large, version-controlled code lists may live in separate files sourced by setup.R.
Place reusable helpers in R/functions.R, or organized subdirectories when warranted. Prefer explicit function arguments over dependence on global objects.
Avoid setwd(), machine-specific absolute paths, and writes outside designated project outputs. Locate restricted USRDS inputs through usRds’s directory configuration.
No results in the repository. No script (exploratory or definitive) or comment, commit message, issue, pull-request text or review report contains results, counts or data values from restricted data unless they are cleared for release. Check before every commit and post, since a public repository publishes everything pushed to it, on any branch. Numbers quoted from the published paper are public and may be cited.

Chunk labels
Scripts are divided into labelled sections so Quarto can reuse code without copying it:
## ---- cryptococcus-claims

Label logical steps with descriptive kebab-case identifiers unique across scripts; a duplicate silently picks up the wrong code. A label covers code up to the next label.
Before renaming or removing a label, check the .qmd pages that reference it.
Labels are comments; the underlying R scripts must remain executable through main.R.

Variable labels

Label analytical variables with human-readable descriptions (for example, labelled::set_variable_labels()).
For USRDS fields, prefer usRds::apply_usrds_varlabels() and usRds::apply_usrds_factors() rather than duplicating source labels.
Label derived variables where created, including units and time windows where relevant.

Quarto website
The site documents the code. It does not run the analysis. Exploratory scripts need no page.

_quarto.yml, index.qmd, 404.qmd (the page GitHub Pages shows for a missing address) and styles.css sit at the root; quarto/ has one page per definitive script, named after it (for example, quarto/create_cohort.qmd for R/create_cohort.R), plus the Study design and methods, Published results (quarto/results.qmd: the paper’s tables and figures as printed, with notes on apparent errors; its notice says they are reproduced from the article under its license, not produced by this code), About and project-document pages (including quarto/usrds-coverage.qmd, which shows references/usrds-coverage.md). Background pages are added once their content is written; the Home page carries a short background until then. The custom-callout extension in _extensions/ provides the Rcode, Results and Pending callouts.
Visual cues. Each kind of page has one sidebar icon, coloured by styles.css, and pages mark the same kind of content with the callout of that colour: background book (blue); study design and methods diagram-3 (orange); R code laptop (pink, Rcode 💻); results clipboard-data (green, Results 📊); project documents file-earmark-ruled (grey). Give every new page the icon of its kind.
Provisional content. quarto/_pending.lua highlights in yellow every paragraph that starts with Decision pending: or, in the plan, Open:, and any [text]{.pending}, and adds a ⏳ Pending callout to pages that have a mark. Mark only what an open decision could change, link the decision issue, and remove the mark when the decision is settled.
Project documents. analysis-plan.md, ARCHITECTURE.md, AGENTS.md and REPOSITORY-BLUEPRINT.md are shown on the site by pages in quarto/ that only include the root file, which stays the one source: edit the root file, not the page.
Each script page loads its script with knitr::read_chunk("../R/<script>.R") in a hidden chunk and shows each labelled section with #| eval: false, with prose explaining what the section does and why, without duplicating source code. Pages link to the script on GitHub and to the scripts it depends on.
Never evaluate analysis code in the site. Pages render without restricted data. Only the read_chunk() imports, the Architecture page’s chunk that reads ARCHITECTURE.md, site helpers that read code or text, and results pages that read cleared outputs run. Review any proposed publication of aggregate results separately for disclosure compliance.
Publishing. The site renders to docs/, which is not committed: a GitHub Actions workflow (.github/workflows/publish.yml) renders it on every push to main and publishes it to the gh-pages branch, which GitHub Pages serves. On a pull request the workflow only renders, as a check that every page builds.
When you add a definitive script, add its page and sidebar entry in the same pull request. Prose must match the code: if a change alters what a section does, or its chunk labels, update its explanation and navigation in the same pull request.

Outputs

R/tables.R and R/figures.R may create outputs directly or orchestrate specialized scripts, exporting to tables/ and figures/.
tables/ and figures/ are gitignored until USRDS review before publication clears them for release, because they come from restricted data: agents may not open them (see Restricted data). Commit cleared, nonrestricted results only when intentional. Disclosure rules apply to all outputs.
Published figures need alt text.
README.Rmd is the source of README.md; edit the .Rmd and re-knit.

Restricted data (applies to everyone)
USRDS and Medicare data are governed by a data use agreement (DUA). Applicable DUA requirements take precedence over convenience or automation. The Access column of “Data sources” says which sources are restricted. For each restricted source:

Never commit data, extracts, person-level data objects, or saved objects or outputs derived from patient-level records. Keep restricted source data outside the repository, and review output paths and .gitignore before adding new output types.
AI agents never read restricted data. Anything an agent opens, prints, or summarizes is sent to the model provider. Agents do not open data files or patient-level objects, print rows, or display identifiers (including USRDS IDs), person-level dates, or ZIP codes. Agents also do not open outputs from restricted data that are not yet cleared for release (for example tables/ and figures/ while they are ignored). Agents write code, review it, and run it on synthetic data; results on real data are produced by an authorized person in an authorized environment. A request to execute a pipeline does not itself provide authorization. The only exception is what the Data sources table explicitly allows for a source, and only within those words.
Synthetic data are built in code, labelled as synthetic, and never derived from real records.
Disclosure. Prevent disclosure of counts 1–10 in tables, figures, flowcharts, or prose, including counts recoverable by subtraction or complementary cells. Follow the applicable DUA’s exact dissemination rules. Check every output before it leaves the approved environment, including scripts, comments, commit messages, issues, pull-request text and review reports (see R scripts).
Credentials and paid APIs. Never commit keys, tokens, or .Renviron. Ask before paid, bulk, or uncached API calls.

Look in usRds first
The usRds package is the first place to look for USRDS file loading, claims extraction, claim types, diagnosis dates, Medicare coverage, cohort helpers, and costs.

Check its documentation, known limitations, and open issues before reproducing functionality locally.
Raise generally reusable defects or enhancements in usRds; prefer fixes there. Temporary project-specific wrappers must identify the upstream issue and be reconsidered when resolved.
When this analysis depends on a pending usRds enhancement or correction, track the study-specific implementation task here and link it to the corresponding usRds issue.
Record the usRds version or commit used for any result.

USRDS data facts
Data available to this project: the maintainer’s USRDS extract begins on 2006-01-01; there are no records before that date (maintainer, 2026-11-10). Never write a rule, window, lookback or synthetic record that depends on earlier data, and check a lookback against this date before proposing it. The end of the death data is set per release in death_data_end_date (R/setup.R).
Sources: the Researcher’s Guide, Appendix B, and Appendix C for the specific USRDS release being analyzed. The summary below is a starting point, not a replacement for release-appropriate documentation. Obtain the applicable public documents from the NIDDK Researcher’s Guide page. Consult usRds for machine-readable variable labels and formats.
Institutional (IN) claims include inpatient, outpatient, skilled nursing facility, home health, and hospice services.

HCFASAF historically distinguishes I inpatient, O outpatient, N SNF, H home health, and S hospice; older data can include M for REBUS inpatient stays.
Since 2002, corresponding file families include ip_*, op_*, sn_*, hh_*, and hs_*, generally with CLM, DXP, and DET records. Confirm structure for the release.
Institutional claim identifiers include USRDS_ID, CLM_FROM, and SEQ_KEYC; verify the applicable key in source documentation.

Physician/supplier (PS) claims have CLM, LINE, and DX sources.

Claim lines are not necessarily distinct encounters. Define and validate episode grouping before counting services; distinguish diagnoses, procedures, and claim-level versus line-level records.
Physician/supplier services are not synonymous with outpatient care.

Claims year: claims can be assigned by service end date rather than start date; verify against release documentation and account for claims crossing year boundaries.
2025-release data currency (illustrative only; re-verify for the release used): claims complete through 2023-12-31 except the Q1 2024 inpatient file; core files including death dates extend through 2024-12-31. Do not infer contemporaneous coverage of claims and vital status.
Payer history (payhist): payer categories and Medicare FFS observability must be verified against the release-specific guide. The primary versus sensitivity coverage definitions are prescribed in analysis-plan.md, not here. Pay attention to Medicare Advantage, Medicare secondary payer categories, uncovered days, and Medicare entitlement transitions after transplantation.
ICD transition: ICD-9-CM applies before 2015-10-01; ICD-10-CM and ICD-10-PCS on or after that date. Codes may omit decimals. Establish the date controlling the code system for claims spanning the transition, and verify against official code-set definitions.
Unclear variables: consult the relevant Appendix B/C and source code documentation rather than inferring meaning from variable names.

Coding conventions

Build descriptive flowchart text from centrally defined parameters so labels cannot become stale when an analysis window changes.
Code lists: maintain code type, coding system, category, and exact/prefix matching; verify against official coding sources. Distinguish outcome from opportunity codes and personal-history from symptom codes. Do not invent clinical definitions or variables. Check category overlaps and clinically justified exceptions rather than assuming all codes are mutually exclusive.
Cohort flow: every patient-level inclusion or exclusion goes through fc_filter() in the flowchart workflow. Do not drop rows from $data outside the flowchart; the diagram must reproduce the cohort exactly.
Joins: specify join keys and expected relationships. Check row multiplication, particularly after interval joins, and define handling of missing or unmatched records explicitly.
Dates and windows: implement the boundaries prespecified in the analysis plan; test boundary cases on synthetic data.
Code that turns model output into reported numbers lives in named functions in R/functions.R, tested on synthetic data with a known answer.
Package APIs: read the help page and NEWS for the installed version before calling a package; don’t write calls from memory.
Style: use readable tidyverse conventions. Related readability improvements may accompany functional changes; keep unrelated large-scale formatting separate.

Checks for any change
Before presenting changes for review or seeking commit approval, perform the applicable checks below. Report which checks were completed, which were not, and any limitations.
Every change

Plan: does the change implement the plan as written, and does it leave every open decision open?
Data sources: does it use usRds’s functions, and does their documented behavior match what the plan needs?
Package APIs: for new or changed calls to a package, does the pull request name the installed version and the help page or NEWS entry relied on?
Reported numbers: does each estimate match the plan’s estimand, and do tables, figures, and site prose say what the code actually computes?
Disclosure: search every changed tracked file, and the commit messages and pull-request text, for dates, record IDs, names, absolute paths and numbers that could come from restricted data. Read each hit in context; legitimate ones (plan dates, deciders’ names, synthetic examples) stay.

Cohort construction

Do the order, denominator, and labels of flowchart steps reflect the actual conditions?
Are the cohort counts reproducible from the operations shown?
Is downstream analysis based on the final flowchart dataset?

Claims and case definitions

Which claim files, claim types, diagnosis fields, and date fields are used?
Are exact/prefix matching and ICD-9/ICD-10 date transitions handled appropriately?
Can history codes, rule-out diagnoses, or outcome codes contaminate opportunities?

Windows and coverage

Does index ascertainment agree with the analysis plan?
Are date-window boundaries correct and inclusive where specified?
Does eligible Medicare coverage span the entire required observation period, with adjacent spans joined without allowing gaps?

Transplant timing

Are first and repeat transplants distinguished where the analysis requires them?
Are transplant dates and characteristics drawn from the correct episode according to the analysis plan?
Are graft failure and repeat transplants treated as prespecified?

Residence and facility

Is residence information valid for the relevant date?
Is facility information aligned to the appropriate year and transplant center?
Are historical identifiers and changes in identifiers accounted for?

Structure and documentation

Does ARCHITECTURE.md describe current scripts and data flow when structural changes warrant an update?
Are chunk labels unique, and do Quarto pages continue to find the labels they reference?
Does every definitive script have a Quarto page and sidebar entry, with matching chunk labels? Were affected pages and navigation updated?
Does any site chunk evaluate analysis code, and are derived variables labeled?

Execution

Does main.R run from a clean session, using suitable relative paths?
Are machine-specific absolute paths or hard-coded restricted-data directories absent?
Are package versions and saved intermediates documented and checked for staleness?

Validation on real data (by an authorized person only; share only permitted, disclosure-reviewed aggregate findings)

Row counts before and after interval joins.
Counts of people with multiple matching coverage or residence spans.
Case counts by ICD-9 versus ICD-10 era and by claim type.

Working with agents

Autonomy. The person directing an agent sets its working style (review only, step by step, or hands-off) in their own instructions, and may add stricter rules; those take precedence. Without a style, an agent works step by step. At most, an agent may edit code and documentation, add scripts and tests, run code and render the site on synthetic data, and commit to a branch and open a pull request.
Decisions. Anyone, including an agent, may add options and evidence to a decision issue. A decider states the choice in the issue. Agents implement decisions; they never choose among options on their own, in the issue, the plan, or the code.
Every agent, under any autonomy: never merges a pull request; follows the restricted-data rules; asks before running the full pipeline or making expensive external/API calls (approval for these does not override DUA restrictions); shows a person the exact text before posting or sending anything as them, unless that person’s own instructions waive this; and proposes another way of writing something already agreed before committing it.
Pull requests opened by an agent are focused. Each says which plan section or issue it addresses, what was checked, and whether by running code on synthetic data or by reading only. Synthetic results are never described as clinical results.
Scientific citations: maintain verified references in root-level references.bib; cite methodological sources in analysis-plan.md and technical references with the corresponding implementation documentation. Verify bibliographic metadata, source support for claims, and compatibility with the data release being analyzed.

title: About
text:
This project replicates Fiorica et al. 20251, a study of mortality among kidney transplant recipients hospitalized with cryptococcosis, as the paper describes it. It uses the usRds package and assesses how well that package covers the paper’s methods. The analysis is in progress, and no results from USRDS data are on this site.

Vagish Hemmige (maintainer; makes the scientific decisions)

Open decisions are listed as decision issues.

title: About
text:
This repository
R/main.R runs the scripts in order. They reach the USRDS data through the usRds package. The data are restricted under the USRDS data use agreement, so they are not in the repository. The analysis runs only on a machine with authorized access.
Contributions follow the rules in AGENTS.md. Known issues and open decisions are tracked in Issues.

title: About
text:
How this website was created
The site is built with Quarto from the analysis scripts themselves. Each code page imports the labelled sections of its script from R/ and shows them with an explanation. The site never runs the analysis, so it builds without the analysis data.
The repository is maintained with the R Analysis Workflow plugin and with AI assistants (Claude). They work only on code, documentation and synthetic data, never on USRDS data, and scientific decisions stay with the maintainer.
Four documents describe the project, plus a coverage assessment:

Analysis plan: what the analysis is meant to do, and why.
usRds coverage: each step of the paper mapped to usRds functions, and what is missing.
Architecture: how the code does it.
AGENTS.md: how people and AI assistants work on the project.
Repository blueprint: the layout every project of this kind starts from.

title: About
text:
Pages

Background: Clinical background, Data sources and Statistical methods, for readers new to the disease, the data or the methods.
Study design and methods: the study’s choices in plain language, with the alternatives considered.
Differences from the reconstruction: where this analysis departs from the 2025 reconstruction of the original analysis, and why.
Code, setup and helpers: Setup (packages and shared constants), Code lists (the diagnosis, procedure and billing codes), Functions (helper functions, including those that fill usRds gaps) and Figure style (the house style for figures).
Code, in the order it runs: 1. Building the cohort, 2. Covariates, 3. Outcomes and 4. Survival and models, then Tables and Figures.
Published results: the paper’s figures and tables and its supplement, as published.

title: Published results
text:
Notes on the published results
These are kept above as printed. Each is listed so that this analysis’s outputs can be compared with what was intended. Every percentage was recomputed from its count and column size.
How percentages are printed

Most percentages are cut to one decimal place rather than rounded: for example, 204 of 280 (72.86%) is printed 72.8, and 449 of 985 (45.58%) is printed 45.5. This analysis’s tables round, so many of its percentages will differ from the published ones by 0.1 even when the counts agree.
Where a variable has missing values, percentages use the people with known values, although the table gives a denominator only for CMV serostatus and pretransplant dialysis. For example, the race rows sum to 1,263, not 1,265, and 655 of 983 (66.6%) matches the printed White survivor percentage where 655 of 985 (66.5%) would not; Hispanic ethnicity implies about 1,243 people with known ethnicity. In Table 2, the percentages imply about 1,234 people with drug records at transplant and about 1,068 at follow-up.

Table 1

Lung procedures: the survivor and death cells appear swapped. 84 (30) fits the 280 deaths (84/280 is 30.0%), and 270 (27.4) fits the 985 survivors (270/985 is 27.4%); read as printed (84/985 and 270/280), they would be 8.5% and 96.4%. The total, 354, is their sum.
Rejection episodes, survivors: 144 is printed as 14.2%; 144/985 is 14.6%. A denominator that gives 14.2% would be over 1,000, more than the 985 survivors. The total (178, 14%) and the deaths (34, 12.1%) match their counts.
US region: the four regions sum to 1,257 of 1,265; the table has no row for the other 8. This analysis shows Outside and Unknown as their own rows (plan §5, #12).
Continuous variables: the Methods describe continuous variables as mean ± SD; time since the last transplant is given as median (IQR), and the number of transplants as median (min–max), without a comparison by group.

Table 2

MMF at transplant, total: 1,121 is printed as 90.2%. The row’s own survivor and death percentages imply about 958 and 275 people with records, so 1,121 of about 1,233 (90.9%). The total is an average of the two groups weighted by their size, so with about 3.5 survivors for each death it should lie near the survivors’ 91.1%, not near the deaths’ 90.1%.

Figures

Figure 1 shows the denominators and the final cohort but none of the exclusions the Methods describe (age, cryptococcosis before transplant). “Hospitalizations” could mean hospital records or stays merged from overlapping records; this analysis merges records into stays.
Figure 2 gives only the number at risk, at 5-year intervals, and no confidence band; the 22% in its label is the share who died within 6 months (280 of 1,265), not a reading from the curve.
Figure 3 uses a linear axis, on which an odds ratio of 0.5 and one of 2 look unequal although they are the same size of effect in opposite directions. It labels the time variable “Posttransplant ≥2 years” where the Results say “more than 2 years”; counted in whole days against 2 × 365.25 days, the two pick out the same people. No model N or number of deaths is given.

Text and tables

The Results give male sex in survivors as 66.3% and CMV seropositivity as 70.7%; Table 1 gives 66.2% and 70.6%, the same counts cut rather than rounded.
The Methods take immunosuppression from “the first post-transplant visit”, obtained “using relevant billing codes”; the Results and Discussion refer to a 1-year follow-up. This analysis uses the UNOS records and the earliest follow-up report (plan §5, #2).
The Methods name CPT codes for procedures; Supplementary Table 1 lists ICD procedure codes (plan §5, #5).
The Limitations say cases were identified by 2 ICD-9 codes; the case definition in Supplementary Table 1 also lists ICD-10-CM codes (plan §5).

title: Study design and methods
text:
PendingProvisional



Text highlighted like this is provisional: it depends on a decision the analysis plan has not yet made.
This page explains, in plain language and without code, what this study chose and why. The formal specification is the analysis plan; each section below ends by linking the part of the plan that governs it. Four kinds of note mark where the description stands:

title: Study design and methods
section: The question and the design in brief
text:
The question and the design in brief
The study asks how many kidney transplant recipients die within 6 months of being hospitalized with cryptococcosis, and which characteristics are associated with dying. It follows recipients from their first cryptococcosis hospitalization after transplant. It compares those who died within 6 months with those who survived, so it describes associations rather than causes.
This project rebuilds the published study from its paper and supplement, and the paper is the specification. Where the paper is silent, the choice is made openly in a decision issue rather than borrowed from a later reconstruction of the original code.
Specified in: Scope, §1 Objective, §2 Design.

title: Study design and methods
text:
Finding the cryptococcosis hospitalizations
A hospitalization counts if a cryptococcosis code appears in any of its diagnosis positions, not only the principal diagnosis. The stays come from the USRDS hospitalization files. These are the inpatient part of the Medicare institutional claims, already organised by stay, and they carry the details the study needs: ICU days, procedures and discharge status. Hospital records that overlap in time are treated as one stay. A stay counts only if it began on or after the first transplant: a stay that began before it, even if it continued past the transplant, is cryptococcosis before transplant, which the paper excludes.
Alternatives considered:

Medicare institutional claims instead of the hospitalization files. Claims are the raw billing records; the hospitalization files are built from them and already grouped into stays. Using claims would exercise more of the usRds package, but it would add nothing as a check, because the USRDS Researcher’s Guide describes the hospitalization files as a subset of the claims. Not done (#1).
Which code set applies around October 2015. A stay that straddles the switch from ICD-9 to ICD-10 is coded by its discharge date, which is Medicare’s rule; its admission date would be the other choice (#8).
Where the code lists come from. The paper’s supplement and the 2025 reconstruction list the same codes, with a few gaps: neither lists codes for ventriculoperitoneal shunt, which the paper reports, so that list was rebuilt from the official code sets; and the reconstruction’s diabetes codes, read literally, would miss most ICD-10 diabetes codes, so they are matched as open prefixes, as the supplement does (#8).

Specified in: §3 Data source, §5.

title: Study design and methods
text:
Who is included
The cohort is adults aged 18 to 90 with a kidney or kidney–pancreas transplant whose first cryptococcosis hospitalization came after their transplant. People who had a cryptococcosis claim before their first transplant are excluded. The paper’s cohort is described as having Medicare as primary insurance. Because every index stay is a Medicare-paid record, no separate payer check is applied. An explicit check is described as a possible variation.
A cryptococcosis claim before the first transplant excludes the person: a hospital record or a physician’s bill, and one is enough. Earlier claims can only be seen while someone had Medicare, which recipients on dialysis usually did and those transplanted before dialysis often did not.
Alternatives considered:

Checking Medicare as primary payer. The paper’s cohort had Medicare as primary insurance but the paper gives no time window. One could require it on the admission date, for the year before, or from transplant onward; a longer window makes claims-based measures more complete and shrinks the cohort. Here no explicit check is made, and the check is kept as a variation (#3).
A stay that begins before the first transplant and ends after it. The reconstruction kept such stays, with time since transplant set to zero. The paper excludes cryptococcosis before transplant, so here they are excluded (#4).
How many earlier claims to require, and of what kind. Counting only hospital stays would miss cryptococcosis treated outside hospital. Requiring two or more claims would spare people with a single rule-out code, the way many studies define a case. For excluding an earlier condition, though, one claim is the usual rule, and a clinician billing for cryptococcosis before transplant is itself a reason to doubt that the later episode is new (#4;1).
Alaska and Hawaii. They could be counted in the West census region; here they are grouped with the territories as “Outside”, as in the reconstruction, because they are hard to compare with the mainland for a study like this. No one is excluded for where they live (#12).

Specified in: §4 Study population, §9.

title: Study design and methods
text:
What is measured
Characteristics come from three places:

the index stay itself: meningitis or not, acute kidney injury, diabetes, cirrhosis, ICU admission and procedures;
USRDS and UNOS transplant records: transplant history, BMI, pretransplant dialysis, HIV and CMV status, rejection;
earlier hospitalizations: transplant complications.

For someone with more than one transplant, the registry information comes from their most recent transplant before the cryptococcosis hospitalization, because that is the graft and drug regimen they were living with. Acute rejection counts any recorded episode, treated or not, at that transplant or at a follow-up visit before the hospitalization. The registry is the source; hospital claims coded for rejection are an alternative the plan describes but does not use.
Immunosuppressive drugs come from the transplant registry records (UNOS) held in USRDS, at transplant and at the first follow-up visit after transplant, as the paper’s Methods describe. The paper also mentions billing codes; those may be revisited as the source (#2).

Decision pending: whether physician (CPT) billing codes for procedures are used as well as the hospital’s ICD procedure codes (#5).

Alternatives considered:

Which transplant’s records to use. The reconstruction used the first transplant. For someone transplanted more than once, the most recent transplant before the hospitalization describes the graft and drugs they had at the time, so that one is used (#12).
Acute rejection from the registry or from claims. The registry records any episode at transplant or follow-up. Hospital claims coded for kidney transplant rejection are the alternative, but ICD-9 has no code specific to rejection, so a claims definition would only work from October 2015 (#12; plan §9).
Immunosuppression from the registry or from billing codes. The paper’s Methods mention billing codes, and its supplement lists drug billing codes for cyclosporine and tacrolimus; the reconstruction used the registry. Billing codes would show drugs actually dispensed, but only for some drugs and only where Medicare paid. The registry is used, at transplant and at the first follow-up visit, as the paper’s Methods describe. The paper’s Discussion speaks of a “1-year follow-up”; the Methods’ “first post-transplant visit” is followed (#2).

Specified in: §5.

title: Study design and methods
text:
Outcome and analysis
The main outcome is death from any cause within 180 days of admission. The methods follow the paper:

survivors and non-survivors are compared;
survival over time is drawn as a Kaplan–Meier curve;
the factors associated with death are found with logistic regression, using backward elimination as the paper did.

The paper’s own final model is also refitted exactly as published, with its eight characteristics, so its odds ratios can be compared with the published ones directly (Table 4).
Alternatives considered:

Rerunning the selection, or fitting the published model. Rerunning backward elimination repeats what the paper did, but a small change in the data can change which characteristics survive, and then the odds ratios cannot be compared one for one. Fitting the paper’s eight characteristics directly compares the estimates, but not the selection. Both are done, and Table 4 shows them side by side.
Backward elimination at all. Selecting variables by their P values gives P values that look smaller than they should and a model that may not repeat in other data. Choosing the variables beforehand on clinical grounds, or using penalized regression, are the usual alternatives. Elimination is kept because the aim is to repeat the paper; its limits are listed in plan §11.
How each step is tested. A characteristic with several categories (such as region) gets one joint test, not one per category, and every step uses the same people: everyone with all candidates known. This is how Stata, the paper’s software, does it. Testing with likelihood ratios, or letting the sample grow as variables are removed, are reasonable alternatives that can give a different final model.

Specified in: §7 Outcomes, §8 Statistical analysis.

title: Figure style
text: The house style for figures: one theme with its colors, shapes and line types, readable labels, and one way to save a figure at its printed size. The file is copied unchanged from the maintainer’s COHERO analysis, so figures look the same across his projects.

title: Figure style
Figure style
text:
Palettes
A palette is the ordered set of colors (or shapes, or line types) given to the groups in a figure. The colors are the Okabe-Ito set, chosen to stay distinguishable for people with the common kinds of color-vision deficiency, with a neutral dark gray first for a reference group. Groups also differ by point shape and line type, so a figure still works in grayscale and never relies on color alone. This study’s figures each show a single series, which takes the first color after the gray.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Okabe-Ito colors (safe for the common kinds of color-vision deficiency),
# with a neutral dark gray first: the first group of any factor, such as the
# control arm or a reference level, is drawn in gray and the second in blue
okabe_ito <- unname(grDevices::palette.colors(palette = "Okabe-Ito"))
publication_colors <- c("#555555", okabe_ito[c(6, 7, 4, 2, 8, 3, 5)])

# Shapes and line types differ too, so groups never rely on color alone.
# Filled shapes 21-25 take a white fill, so overlapping points stay visible.
publication_shapes <- c(21, 24, 22, 23, 25)
publication_linetypes <- c("22", "solid", "42", "12", "4212")

title: Figure style
text:
The publication theme
A theme controls everything in a figure that is not data: background, gridlines, text sizes, legend position. theme_publication() keeps only what helps a reader: light horizontal gridlines to read values against, thin axis lines, no panel border. It also carries the palettes above, so a figure needs no color settings of its own. Text sizes are set for the printed figure (9 points by default), so a figure should be saved at the size it will be printed.


Click to show/hide R Code
# A quiet theme for print: no panel border, light horizontal gridlines only,
# thin axis lines, text sized for the printed figure. The legend sits above
# the panel; figures that name their groups on the plot itself remove it.
theme_publication <- function(base_size = 9, base_family = "",
                              header_family = NULL) {
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(
    base_size = base_size,
    base_family = base_family,
    header_family = header_family
  ) +
    ggplot2::theme(
      panel.grid.minor = ggplot2::element_blank(),
      panel.grid.major.x = ggplot2::element_blank(),
      panel.grid.major.y = ggplot2::element_line(
        color = "gray90", linewidth = 0.3
      ),
      axis.line.x = ggplot2::element_line(color = "gray30", linewidth = 0.3),
      axis.ticks.x = ggplot2::element_line(color = "gray30", linewidth = 0.3),
      axis.title = ggplot2::element_text(color = "gray20"),
      axis.text = ggplot2::element_text(color = "gray30"),
      strip.text = ggplot2::element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0),
      plot.title = ggplot2::element_text(face = "bold"),
      plot.title.position = "plot",
      plot.caption = ggplot2::element_text(color = "gray35", hjust = 0),
      plot.caption.position = "plot",
      legend.position = "top",
      legend.justification = "left",
      palette.color.discrete = publication_colors,
      palette.fill.discrete = publication_colors,
      palette.shape.discrete = scales::pal_manual(publication_shapes),
      palette.linetype.discrete = publication_linetypes
    )
}

title: Figure style
Figure style
text:
Saving a figure
save_figure() writes a figure at its printed size in millimetres, in each format needed: PDF and SVG, which keep lines and text sharp at any zoom, for journals; and PNG for the website. Figures 2 and 3 are saved with it.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Save a figure at its printed size, in millimetres: PDF (cairo, which embeds
# fonts and handles symbols such as the dagger) and SVG for journals, PNG
# (ragg) for the website. Returns the paths written.
save_figure <- function(plot, file, width, height,
                        formats = c("pdf", "svg", "png"), dpi = 600) {
  devices <- list(
    pdf = grDevices::cairo_pdf,
    svg = svglite::svglite,
    png = ragg::agg_png
  )
  paths <- paste0(file, ".", formats)
  for (i in seq_along(formats)) {
    ggplot2::ggsave(
      paths[i], plot,
      device = devices[[formats[i]]],
      width = width, height = height, units = "mm", dpi = dpi,
      bg = "white"
    )
  }
  invisible(paths)
}

title: Differences from the reconstruction
text:
The original analysis was run in Stata (the paper also lists R and RStudio among its software), and that code is no longer available. In 2025 the maintainer rebuilt it in R as an R Markdown file dated 25 March 2025, his best reconstruction of what was done. That file did not produce the published numbers, and it is not in this repository, because of how it was put together. The specification for this analysis is the paper and its supplement1; the reconstruction is secondary evidence.
This page lists every place where this analysis differs from the reconstruction, and every place where the reconstruction differs from the paper. It describes the reconstruction without reproducing it. Each entry is one of five kinds:

title: Differences from the reconstruction

Finding the hospitalizations
