PendingProvisional



Text highlighted like this is provisional: it depends on a decision the analysis plan has not yet made.
This script attaches the packages and defines the constants every other script uses.

title: Setup
text:
Packages
The analysis uses the tidyverse for data handling. usRds is the access package for the USRDS files: it locates the files on the machine that holds them and loads or extracts from them. The coverage assessment records which steps it does. flowchart builds the cohort flow diagram (Figure 1), survival the Kaplan–Meier curve (Figure 2), and labelled the variable labels.


Click to show/hide R Code
library(tidyverse)  # dplyr, tidyr, stringr, lubridate and friends
library(usRds)      # USRDS file loading and claims extraction
library(flowchart)  # cohort flow diagram (Figure 1)
library(survival)   # Kaplan-Meier (Figure 2)
library(labelled)   # variable labels

title: Setup
text:
Constants
These are the study’s fixed parameters, each tied to the section of the analysis plan that sets it:

the admission window for the index hospitalization, 2006–2016 (§3);
the age range, 18 to 90 years inclusive (§4);
the 180-day mortality window, in which a death on day 180 counts (§7);
the ICD-10 transition date (§5);
the 2-year cut-off for time since transplant in the model (§5).

Scripts use these names rather than typing the numbers again.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Study window for the index hospitalization admission date (plan §3)
study_start_date <- as.Date("2006-01-01")
study_end_date <- as.Date("2016-12-31")

# Calendar years of physician/supplier claims searched for cryptococcosis
# before the first transplant (plan §4, step 4): the study years, which is
# where the data begin (coverage map, step 10).
physician_claim_years <- seq(
  lubridate::year(study_start_date),
  lubridate::year(study_end_date)
)

# Age at index admission, in years, inclusive (plan §4, step 6)
age_min <- 18
age_max <- 90

# Primary outcome window: death within this many days of index admission;
# a death on day 180 counts (plan §7)
mortality_window_days <- 180

# ICD-9-CM before this date, ICD-10-CM/PCS on or after (plan §5)
icd10_start_date <- as.Date("2015-10-01")

# Time since most recent transplant is dichotomized at this many years for the
# multivariable model (plan §5)
years_since_transplant_cutoff <- 2

title: Setup
text:
Code lists
The code lists are long, so they live in their own script; see Code lists.


Click to show/hide R Code
source("R/code_lists.R")

title: Setup
text:
Hospitalization file columns
The two USRDS hospitalization files store diagnoses differently, according to Appendix B of the Researcher’s Guide (2024):

hosp_to2009 holds up to 10 diagnosis codes, in HSDIAG1–HSDIAG10. Its PRIMDIAG is only a yes/no flag saying whether the first diagnosis is the principal one.
hosp_2010on holds the principal diagnosis code in PRIMDIAG and up to 26 more in HSDIAG1–HSDIAG26.

These constants name the columns that hold codes in each file, so a search never treats the old yes/no flag as a code.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Diagnosis code columns in the two USRDS hospitalization files (Researcher's
# Guide 2024, Appendix B). In hosp_to2009, PRIMDIAG is a Y/N flag ("first
# diagnosis is primary"), not a code, so only HSDIAG1-HSDIAG10 hold codes; in
# hosp_2010on, PRIMDIAG is the principal diagnosis code.
hosp_to2009_dx_columns <- str_c("HSDIAG", 1:10)
hosp_2010on_dx_columns <- c("PRIMDIAG", str_c("HSDIAG", 1:26))
hosp_to2009_proc_columns <- str_c("HSSURG", 1:10)
hosp_2010on_proc_columns <- str_c("HSSURG", 1:25)

title: Setup
text:
UNOS keys and covariate concepts
The UNOS files link to one another by identifiers whose names changed between USRDS releases: the 2024 release adds _CODE to each. The registration key here, TRR_ID, is the one the reconstruction used with this project’s release. The follow-up key, TRRFU_ID, has not been checked against that release.

Decision pending: the follow-up key name has to be confirmed against Appendix B for the release in use before the covariates script is run.

The concept lists name which diagnoses and procedures are flagged on the index stay.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Keys linking the UNOS files. The registration key is the one the
# reconstruction uses (TRR_ID), matching the maintainer's release. The
# follow-up key is NOT VERIFIED: the 2024 layout names it TRRFU_ID_CODE
# (and the registration key TRR_ID_CODE); check both against Appendix B for
# the release in use before running.
unos_registration_id <- "TRR_ID"
unos_followup_id <- "TRRFU_ID"

# Concepts flagged on the index stay (diagnoses and procedures) and on earlier
# hospitalizations (plan §5)
index_stay_dx_concepts <- c(
  "cryptococcal_meningitis", "acute_kidney_injury", "diabetes", "cirrhosis"
)
index_stay_proc_concepts <- c(
  "lumbar_puncture", "spinal_procedure", "neurosurgical_procedure",
  "lung_procedure", "vp_shunt"
)

title: Setup
text:
Outcome and model settings
These settings control the outcomes and models:

The end of death data for the USRDS release in use. It is set by whoever runs the analysis, because the paper doesn’t give it and it varies by release.
The age cut-off of 60 that the paper’s model uses.
The P value for backward elimination.
The list of candidate variables: every characteristic in Tables 1 and 2, in the form the paper reports them.
The paper’s final model: its eight variables, with the adjusted odds ratios and confidence intervals it reports, for the comparison in Table 4.


Decision pending: death_data_end_date has to be set for the release in use; the outcomes script stops until it is.



Click to show/hide R Code
# End of death ascertainment for the USRDS release in use: deaths after this
# date are not observed, and survival time is censored here (plan §7). It
# depends on the release, so it is set by whoever runs the analysis; the
# outcome script stops while it is missing.
death_data_end_date <- as.Date(NA)

# Age cut-off used in the paper's model ("age >= 60 years"; plan §8)
age_model_cutoff <- 60

# Significance level for backward elimination (plan §8)
elimination_threshold <- 0.05

# Candidate variables for the bivariable and multivariable models: every
# characteristic in Tables 1 and 2, in model-ready form (plan §8). The paper
# examined "each variable" and entered them all, so there is no entry
# threshold. Drug classes at follow-up are entered as "not on" for
# tacrolimus, as the paper reports it.
model_candidates <- c(
  "age_60_or_older", "sex", "race", "hispanic", "region",
  "cryptococcal_meningitis", "acute_kidney_injury", "diabetes", "cirrhosis",
  "icu_admission", "lumbar_puncture", "spinal_procedure",
  "neurosurgical_procedure", "lung_procedure", "vp_shunt",
  "prior_transplant_complication", "more_than_one_transplant",
  "prior_graft_failure", "over_cutoff_since_transplant", "bmi",
  "pretransplant_dialysis", "hiv_status", "cmv_status", "acute_rejection",
  "tx_antithymocyte_globulin", "tx_alemtuzumab", "tx_il2_receptor_antibody",
  "no_tacrolimus_at_transplant", "tx_cyclosporine", "tx_mycophenolate",
  "tx_mtor_inhibitor", "tx_azathioprine", "tx_steroids",
  "no_tacrolimus_at_followup", "fu_cyclosporine", "fu_mycophenolate",
  "fu_mtor_inhibitor", "fu_azathioprine", "fu_steroids"
)

# The paper's final model: its eight terms with the adjusted odds ratios and
# 95% CIs it reports, in the paper's order (Fiorica et al. 2025, Results;
# plan §8). Fitted as given, beside the backward elimination, to compare
# estimates separately from which variables the selection keeps.
published_model <- tibble::tribble(
  ~term,                            ~published_or, ~published_low, ~published_high,
  "cirrhosis",                       3.1,           1.2,            7.7,
  "icu_admission",                   2.9,           2.0,            4.0,
  "pretransplant_dialysis",          2.7,           1.5,            4.9,
  "no_tacrolimus_at_followup",       2.2,           1.4,            3.3,
  "age_60_or_older",                 2.0,           1.4,            2.8,
  "acute_kidney_injury",             1.7,           1.2,            2.4,
  "over_cutoff_since_transplant",    1.7,           1.1,            2.4,
  "prior_transplant_complication",   1.5,           1.1,            2.2
)
stopifnot(all(published_model$term %in% model_candidates))

load_usrds_file("patients") for death dates; cohort functions not needed
Covered; cohort functions not used, and defects found


19
Logistic regression, Table 1, figures
outside usRds’s scope
Not applicable


—
Infectious diseases specialist claims (legacy Rmd only, not in the paper)
get_PS_specialty()
Covered, with defects

Step details

1. Locate data files
set_USRDS_wd(path) stores the path and maps the files; the map is rebuilt on package load when USRDS_WD is set. The legacy Rmd calls map_USRDS_files() directly, which is now internal (.map_USRDS_files()); scripts should call only set_USRDS_wd(), once, outside the repository (the path is machine-specific).
The mapper recognises six folder names: “ESRD Core”, “ESRD transplant”, “ESRD hospital”, “ESRD PartD”, “ESRD Institution” and “Physician supplier”. The legacy Rmd’s local folders are prefixed with a number (“1) ESRD core”); to verify that the case-sensitive str_detect() matches “ESRD core” (lower-case c) as well as “ESRD Core”.


2. Demographics and death date
load_usrds_file("patients", col_select = c(USRDS_ID, BORN, DIED, STATE, HISPANIC)). apply_usrds_factors() labels coded variables from Appendix C, replacing the legacy Rmd’s hand-written recodes for Hispanic ethnicity. Race and sex in the legacy Rmd come from the tx file (RACE, RSEX), not patients; the plan should name which file each comes from.


3. Transplant history
load_usrds_file("tx", col_select = c(USRDS_ID, TDATE, FAILDATE, TOTTX)) loads one row per transplant. The paper needs, for each patient at the index date: first transplant date, number of transplants and graft failures before the index admission, and time since the most recent transplant. The legacy Rmd pivots to wide format (TDATE_1… TDATE_5) and loops over positions.
The patients file also has TX1DATE (date of first transplant; Appendix B 2024), which could replace the minimum of TDATE; the cohort script uses the tx file, which it needs for transplant history anyway. Gap: a long-format helper, for example summarise_transplant_history(df, index_date), returning those quantities per patient. It is generally reusable: the missed-diagnosis project needs first transplant date too.


4. Index cryptococcosis hospitalization (#1)
Decided in #1: the hospitalization files (hosp_to2009, hosp_2010on), as the legacy Rmd uses. A stay is flagged if PRIMDIAG or any HSDIAG position (10 before 2010, 26 from 2010) is in the cryptococcosis list. The Researcher’s Guide (2024, Appendix B) describes both files as “a subset of the data in the Institutional Claims file”, inpatient stays only and without payment variables, so the institutional-claims route below is noted for completeness, not used.

load_usrds_file("hosp_2010on") works, but reads the whole file before any filtering, and the diagnosis search across wide columns is hand-written.
get_IN_ICD(icd_codes, years) reads the institutional diagnosis files (file roots det<year><letter> in the internal IN_ICD table) with filtering pushed down for Parquet. It returns only USRDS_ID, CODE, CLM_FROM and HCFASAF: no CLM_THRU, no claim key (SEQ_KEYC) and no diagnosis position. So a stay found this way cannot be linked to its discharge status, ICU days or procedures, and principal and secondary diagnoses cannot be told apart.
establish_dx_date() applies a “first inpatient or second outpatient claim” rule, not the paper’s “first hospitalization” rule.

Gaps:


get_HOSP_ICD(icd_codes, years, positions = "any"): searches PRIMDIAG/HSDIAG* with pushdown, and returns one row per stay with its key, dates, DISCSTAT, ICU_DAYS and CCU_DAYS.


Alternatively, an option on get_IN_ICD() to return CLM_THRU, SEQ_KEYC and the diagnosis position, plus a companion that loads the claim header for a set of keys.


Found while writing the cohort script: the two hospitalization files use PRIMDIAG differently (Appendix B 2024). In hosp_to2009 it is a Y/N flag (“first diagnosis is primary”) and the codes are in HSDIAG1–HSDIAG10. In hosp_2010on it is the principal diagnosis code. Searching PRIMDIAG in both, as the legacy Rmd does, is harmless but wrong in meaning. An extractor for these files (gap (a)) should hide that difference; this project handles it with per-file column lists in R/setup.R. Loading with default factor_labels = TRUE would also turn the pre-2010 flag into a factor, so the cohort script loads with factor_labels = FALSE.
To verify:

whether the det files contain procedure codes as well as diagnosis codes in CODE, and if so how they are distinguished;
the SAS branch of .load_individual_file_IN_ICD() omits HCFASAF, so establish_dx_date() would misclassify SAS-sourced claims;
hospitalization file names differ by release; Appendix B for the release in use governs;
which files hold institutional diagnosis codes: in the 2024 layout (Appendix B), inpatient diagnosis and procedure codes are in ip_dxp_<year> (“Diagnosis and Procedure Details”), while get_IN_ICD() reads files with roots det<year><letter>, the name the 2024 layout uses for revenue-line details. Older releases may name files differently.



5. Cryptococcal meningitis on the index stay
B45.1 or 321.0 in any diagnosis position of the index stay, including stays merged with it (step 7). This depends on the stay-level output of step 4. No separate gap.


6. Comorbidities on the index stay
AKI and cirrhosis use exact code lists. Diabetes uses open prefixes (250*, E08*–E13*; plan §5). The reconstruction enumerated stems plus at most two digits instead, which misses most ICD-10-CM diabetes codes; an exact-only matcher pushes code toward that kind of enumeration error. The project matches prefixes with code_matches() in R/functions.R.
Gap: the get_*_ICD() functions match exactly (CODE %in% icd_codes). The package builds an icd_reference table “so that the get_*_ICD functions can use wildcards” (data-raw/DATASET.R), but no exported function uses it yet. A prefix = TRUE option, or an expand_icd_codes("E11", type = "dx") helper backed by icd_reference, would close this.


7. ICU admission and overlapping claims
The legacy Rmd treats hospitalization records whose CLM_FROM falls on or before the previous record’s CLM_THRU as one continuing stay. It sums ICU_DAYS, CCU_DAYS and the procedure and diagnosis flags across up to seven records, and defines ICU admission as any ICU or CCU days.
Gap: collapse_stays(df, gap_days = 0): groups contiguous or overlapping institutional records into episodes, with an episode ID, start and end. It is reusable for readmission and length-of-stay work.


8. Discharge status
The legacy Rmd recodes DISCSTAT by hand into home, other facility, death and still inpatient. To verify: whether Appendix B gives DISCSTAT a format in the hospitalization file, so that apply_usrds_factors() labels it. The grouping into four categories is a study choice, and stays in this project.


9. Procedures on the index stay (#5)
The legacy Rmd counts HSSURG1–HSSURG25 matches against the supplement’s lists. usRds has HCPCS extractors (get_IN_HCPCS(), get_PS_HCPCS()), which cover CPT codes if #5 chooses them. It has no ICD procedure-code extractor. Gap: get_HOSP_procedure(), or a code_type = "procedure" route in step 4(a).


10. Exclude cryptococcosis before first transplant (#4)
Decided under #4: any one cryptococcosis claim, hospital or physician/supplier, before the first transplant excludes the person. Physician/supplier claims: covered by get_PS_ICD(icd_codes, years, usrds_ids), which returns each claim’s dates. Hospital records: the hospitalization files already loaded for step 4 (project code, as there).

Exact codes only. The cryptococcosis list is all exact codes, so get_PS_ICD() finds them; the script stops if a prefix code is ever added, since it would be missed silently (step 6 and usRds#9 for prefix matching).
No check on icd_codes. Passing the code list as a data frame instead of a character vector returns no claims and no warning; found while writing this step. A type check in the package would catch it.
Years. The package’s file list (PS_ICD) maps physician/supplier files from 2006 to 2021, matching where the data begin. For 2013 onward it includes the DME diagnosis files (dme_dx_*) alongside ps_dx_*.
To verify: the 2024 Appendix B layout of PS_DX_* lists no HCFASAF column, but get_PS_ICD() selects it from every file. If the release in use matches that layout, the 2013-onward files would fail to load. The synthetic files include the column, so this is untested.
The legacy Rmd’s filter appears to keep the opposite group from the one the paper describes; the paper’s rule governs.



11. Prior hospitalization for transplant complications
T86.10–T86.12 or 996.81 on a hospitalization before the index admission. Only a date is needed, so get_IN_ICD() filtered to inpatient claims would cover it. Following #1, the analysis uses the hospitalization files, which it already loads for the index stay (R/create_covariates.R), so this route is project code.


12. Medicare as primary payer (#3)
The main analysis applies no Medicare-primary restriction: the paper gives no window or method, the legacy Rmd applies none, and the index stay is itself a Medicare-paid record (#3). The explicit restriction is a variation (plan §9): verify_medicare_primary(df, index_date = "index_admit_date", lookback_days = ...) adds medicare_primary_TF. Covered, so the function is exercised only if the variation is run.


13–14. UNOS registration and follow-up
These load with load_usrds_file(). Kidney-alone and kidney–pancreas recipients are in separate files with different variable names (ACUTE_REJ_EPI vs ACUTE_REJ_EPI_KI), stacked and renamed in project code, as in the legacy Rmd. The follow-up date falls back to FUKIFAIL when FUDATE is missing.
Appendix C (2024, format ACREJEPI): 1 = yes, at least one episode treated; 2 = yes, none treated with an additional agent; 3 = no; 990 and 998 = episodes unknown (carried over from before 2005). The analysis counts 1 or 2 as an episode and 990/998 as missing; the legacy Rmd dropped only 998.
The analysis takes the registration of the most recent transplant on or before the index admission, and that registration’s follow-up reports, linked by the registration key (TRR_ID in the maintainer’s release, from the legacy Rmd; TRR_ID_CODE in 2024).
Gap (small): load_usrds_unos(c("trr", "fu"), organs = c("ki", "kp")), returning stacked, harmonised kidney variables with an organ indicator. To verify: whether apply_usrds_factors() labels ACUTE_REJ_EPI; the scripts load with factor_labels = FALSE and recode from the raw codes.


13a. Acute rejection from UNOS and from claims
The package should support both routes, and this replication assesses both. UNOS (used): loading is covered by load_usrds_file(); choosing the transplant’s registration and follow-up reports relative to an index date, and recoding ACREJEPI, are project code (gap, as step 13). ICD claims (alternative, plan §9; not built): a hospitalization with ICD-10-CM T86.11 could be found with get_IN_ICD() (dates only, inpatient claims; covered) or from the hospitalization files (gap, step 4). ICD-9-CM has no rejection-specific kidney code, so a claims definition works only from October 2015.


15. Immunosuppression from UNOS records (#2)
Decided in #2: immunosuppression at transplant from TXIRUNOS and at the first follow-up from TXIFUNOS (“Immunosuppression at Follow-up – UNOS”, Appendix B 2024), which the legacy Rmd never loads. Both should load with load_usrds_file(). To verify:

that the file mapper finds txifunos;
the join keys: the legacy Rmd joins TXIRUNOS to the registration on TRR_ID, but the 2024 layout has encrypted keys (TRR_ID_CODE; TRRFU_ID_CODE linking TXIFUNOS to the follow-up reports), so key names depend on the release. The scripts take both names from constants in R/setup.R; the follow-up key TRRFU_ID is a guess for the maintainer’s release and must be checked before running.

The legacy Rmd maps RX_CD codes and misspelled free text (DRUG_CD_OSTXT) to drug classes. Checked against Appendix C (format DRUG), every code it maps is labelled correctly, but it misses 57 (generic Myfortic), 58 (generic sirolimus) and 59 (Envarsus XR), which are added (R/code_lists.R). Gap: a verified RX_CD-to-class crosswalk shipped as package data, from Appendix C, so projects don’t re-derive it. The free-text clean-up is study-specific and stays here.


16. Immunosuppression from HCPCS claims (#2)
Not used in the main analysis (#2), but kept in the assessment because the maintainer may revisit it (billing data may be the gold standard). get_PS_HCPCS(c("J7502", "J7515", "J7516", "J7503", "J7507", "J7508", "J7525"), years), plus get_IN_HCPCS() for institutional lines. Covered. The package maps Part D files (a PDE file list exists internally) but has no Part D extractor. Part D is out of scope (#2); if oral tacrolimus from Part D is ever brought in, that is a gap.


17. Age, region and division
Age comes from BORN. STATE uses FIPS codes (Appendix C format STATFIP, which also lists 03 American Samoa and 43 Puerto Rico, older codes). The legacy Rmd maps them to Census regions by hand; territory codes it does not list (for example 66 Guam, 78 Virgin Islands) fall through to missing, which R/code_lists.R corrects by mapping every valid non-state code to “Outside”. It also groups Alaska and Hawaii with the territories, unlike the Census Bureau; the analysis keeps that grouping (#12).
Hispanic ethnicity (format $YNUFMT) codes “no” as 2 or N. The legacy Rmd recoded 0 or N as non-Hispanic, so code 2 would have become missing; the analysis follows the format. Sex and race ($SEXFMT, $RACEFMT) are recoded as in the legacy Rmd.
Gap (small): a state-code crosswalk as package data; and recoding is project code because the scripts load with factor_labels = FALSE. Whether apply_usrds_factors() would label these correctly is to verify.


18. Mortality and survival
Death dates load with load_usrds_file("patients"). Every covariate is fixed and death is the only event, so the survival data needs one row per person (time to death or end of death data, and whether death occurred), which survival::survfit() takes directly. The usRds cohort functions (create_usrds_cohort(), add_cohort_event(), finalize_usrds_cohort(), add_cohort_covariate()) are built for follow-up split by time-varying covariates or repeated events, and the analysis does not use them.
They were probed on synthetic data (sourced from the usRds clone at 3f63750, four people followed 180 days), because a survival analysis with time-varying covariates would rely on them:







Behaviour
Result




Dates passed as a column-name string
Works. A bare column name fails, although the internal helper’s comment says either works.


Death on the start date
Not counted: tmerge events fall in (tstart, tstop], so an event at time 0 is dropped.


Death during follow-up
Follow-up continues after death: add_cohort_event() uses cumevent(), so a second interval from the death to the end keeps the person at risk. A Kaplan–Meier estimate from this overstates survival.


Death on the end date
Counted.


Ending follow-up at death (end_date = earlier of death and end)
Fixes continued follow-up, but stops with “tstart must be < tstop” for a death on the start date.



For death as an outcome, add_cohort_event() therefore needs a terminal-event option (stop follow-up at the event, using event() rather than cumevent()), and same-day events need a convention (for example, half a day). These are listed as follow-ups below.


Cohort selection
The usRds cohort functions handle follow-up time, not entry: create_usrds_cohort() requires a data frame that already has one row per person (it stops on a repeated USRDS_ID), with start and end dates. Finding each person’s index event and applying the exclusions is done in project code: R/create_cohort.R, with helpers in R/functions.R and every exclusion through flowchart. That part is a gap, but a mostly study-specific one. The reusable pieces (searching the hospitalization files, combining records into stays, first transplant date) are already listed as gaps at steps 3, 4 and 7, so no separate usRds follow-up is proposed.


Infectious diseases specialist claims (legacy Rmd only)
get_PS_specialty("44", 2006:2016, DIAG = TRUE, HCPCS = TRUE) works, but has these defects:

leftover print() debugging calls;
the SAS branch pipes into return(temp) before temp exists;
the SAS branch reads by col_select but never converts dates;
the Parquet branch reads the whole file before filtering.

The paper does not use these claims, so they are out of scope for the plan unless a decider adds them.

Package-wide observations
These are not tied to one step, but affect several.

Which copy load_usrds_file() reads. It takes the first registry match (slice(1)). The registry is built CSV first, then SAS, then Parquet. So when a file exists in more than one format, it appears to read the CSV, contradicting the vignette’s statement that Parquet is preferred. To verify on synthetic files.
apply_usrds_varlabels() stops unless metadata_b exists in the global environment. The data are internal to the package, so with var_labels = TRUE it may always fail. apply_usrds_factors() has the same check commented out. To verify.
load_usrds_file() with col_select on Parquet always fails. It reads the column names with arrow::open_dataset(full_path)$head(1). A Dataset is an R6 object, and $head looks for a method of that name on it; there is none, so $head returns NULL and calling it gives “attempt to apply non-function”. head() for a Dataset exists only as an S3 method (head(dataset, 1)). No arrow release has had a $head() method on Dataset (checked all 63 CRAN releases in the cran/arrow mirror, 0.14.1 to 26.0.1), so this branch has never run; it is not a change in arrow. head(arrow::open_dataset(full_path), 1) works, and names(arrow::open_dataset(full_path)$schema) gets the names without reading rows. Found in the synthetic end-to-end run (2026-11-10) and reported as usRds#22. Until it is fixed, the scripts load each file whole with load_usrds_file() and choose columns with select() afterwards, which uses only the package’s public functions but holds every column in memory while loading. When the fix lands, the calls go back to col_select.
load_usrds_file() forces col_select early. is.null(col_select) evaluates the argument outside a selecting function, so col_select = all_of(x) gives tidyselect’s deprecation warning. Capturing it with rlang::enquo() and testing rlang::quo_is_null() would avoid that.
Documentation. Facts this project relies on are not yet in the package documentation: claim-year assignment, ICD transition handling, and hospitalization file structure by release. Where these shape this analysis they are noted in AGENTS.md (“USRDS data facts”); they belong in usRds.

Proposed usRds issues
Possible follow-ups for usRds, listed so the assessment is actionable. Acting on them is outside this project’s scope, and none is opened without the usRds maintainer’s approval.

Hospitalization-file diagnosis extractor with stay-level fields (step 4a).
Claim key, end date and diagnosis position from get_IN_ICD() (step 4b).
Prefix or wildcard matching for ICD codes using icd_reference (step 6).
Combine overlapping or contiguous stays into episodes (step 7).
ICD procedure-code extractor (step 9).
Transplant history relative to an index date (step 3).
Stacked, harmonised UNOS kidney and kidney–pancreas loaders (steps 13–14).
RX_CD immunosuppression crosswalk as package data (step 15).
State code to Census region and division crosswalk (step 17).
Cohort functions for a terminal event (step 18): add_cohort_event() keeps follow-up after death (cumevent()), drops events on the start date, and fails when follow-up ends at a same-day death; the date helper’s comment says bare column names work, but they fail.
Defects: get_PS_specialty() (debug prints, SAS branch); SAS branch of get_IN_ICD() dropping HCFASAF; load_usrds_file() format priority; apply_usrds_varlabels() global-environment check; load_usrds_file() column lookup on Parquet ($head(1), never valid) and early evaluation of col_select (usRds#22).

Provenance

Fiorica et al. 20251, Methods, Tables 1–2, Figures 1–3, and Supplementary Table 1 (open access, PMC12089938).
Legacy analysis Rmd, “Cryptococcus 2025-2-25”, file dated 2025-03-25, supplied by Vagish Hemmige on 2026-11-09. It is his best reconstruction in R of the original analysis, which was run in Stata; the Stata code is no longer available. By the maintainer’s decision it is not kept in this repository, because of its provenance; this document describes it only where it bears on a step.
usRds source at commit 3f63750.

title: Clinical background
text: This page is for readers who want the clinical context before the methods. It summarizes what is known about cryptococcosis after kidney transplant and where the study sits among earlier work.

title: Clinical background
text:
The infection
Cryptococcosis is an infection with the yeast Cryptococcus, usually C. neoformans, which is inhaled from the environment. In people with weakened immunity it can stay in the lungs or spread, most importantly to the brain and its linings as meningitis1,2. Treatment of meningitis and disseminated disease starts with an induction phase of amphotericin B with flucytosine, a lipid formulation of amphotericin B for transplant recipients, followed by fluconazole1–3.

title: Clinical background
text:
After organ transplant
Among invasive fungal infections in solid organ transplant recipients, cryptococcosis is the third most common, after invasive candidiasis and aspergillosis; in a US surveillance network of transplant centres it made up 8% of invasive fungal infections2,4. Unlike most infections after transplant it tends to come late: the median time to onset was 575 days across organs in that network, and 616 days in kidney recipients in a large US hospital-records study4,5.
Which form the infection takes depends partly on immunosuppression. In a review of published cases, recipients on tacrolimus were less likely to have central nervous system involvement6, and over time transplant recipients have more often presented with disease confined to the lungs7.

title: Clinical background
text:
Outcomes
Reported mortality varies with the era, the population and how long people are followed. In a prospective multicentre study of 111 transplant recipients, 14% had died at 90 days8; an earlier review of published cases found an overall death rate of 42%6. Among kidney recipients alone, a French cohort found 32.8% mortality at 12 months9 and a Brazilian cohort 38.3% at 30 days10.
Several factors have been associated with death:

Kidney failure at presentation, in both the case review and the prospective study6,8.
Calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus, cyclosporine): associated with lower mortality in the prospective study8.
Liver disease: end-stage liver disease was a strong predictor of early death in cryptococcosis in general11, and mortality in people with cirrhosis has been high12.

Not every study agrees. In the French kidney cohort, mortality did not differ by whether patients had meningitis9. Compared with patients who had neither HIV nor a transplant, transplant recipients have had similar or lower mortality, in a single-centre study and in US insurance-claims and health-record data13–15.

title: Clinical background
text:
Earlier studies with national data
Earlier USRDS studies looked at how often fungal infections occurred after kidney transplant and what predicted them, grouping cryptococcosis with other fungi or modelling only the risk of infection; neither studied death after cryptococcosis16–18. One of them found maintenance tacrolimus associated with more hospitalizations for fungal infection16; that was about how often infection occurred, not about death. Studies of US hospital records that did single out cryptococcosis were small for transplant recipients: 158 cases across all organs in one5,19.
Fiorica et al. studied 1,265 kidney transplant recipients hospitalized with cryptococcosis from 2006 to 2016, which the authors describe as, to their knowledge, the largest such cohort studied over a 10-year period, and found that 22% had died within 6 months18. This project rebuilds that analysis. No study was found that checks how accurately billing codes identify cryptococcosis (see Data sources), so cases here are cases by code, not by laboratory confirmation.
